chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
The physics of silicon-carbide and gallium-nitride power conversion has delivered CPS Technologies Corporation an unexpectedly large demand tailwind. SiC and GaN switches run hotter and cycle more aggressively than the IGBT devices they replace; the aluminium silicon carbide baseplates and heat spreaders that sit beneath those modules must simultaneously conduct heat away, resist thermal fatigue across tens of thousands of power cycles, and match the ceramic substrate's coefficient of thermal expansion to within a few parts per million. For the past two years that combination of requirements has funnelled procurement toward CPS's Norton, Massachusetts factory in a way that transformed the company's income statement.

## Profile and Franchise

CPS Technologies Corporation (NASDAQ: CPSH) is a specialty metal matrix composites manufacturer headquartered in Norton, Massachusetts. Brian Mackey, President and Chief Executive Officer, leads a small executive team that, as of May 2026, is transitioning its chief financial officer function after Chris Fraser joined the company on 4 May 2026 to succeed the outgoing CFO. The company operates two broad end-market clusters. The first — and now the larger by revenue — is high-power electronics thermal management: AlSiC heat spreaders, baseplates, and packaging substrates sold to manufacturers of SiC and GaN power modules deployed in AI server power-supply units, electric-vehicle traction inverters, RF power amplifiers, and rail-traction converters. The second is defence and armour: HybridTech Armor® composite panels for naval vessels, hermetic packaging for harsh-environment electronics, and small-business innovation research programmes spanning Army rotorcraft and amphibious vehicle platforms.

## Heritage: Lanxide Licensing and the AlSiC Moat

CPS was founded in 1984 and began producing AlSiC composites commercially in the mid-1990s under licence and cross-licence from Lanxide Corporation legacy intellectual property. Lanxide, the Delaware materials pioneer, had demonstrated that pressure-infiltrated aluminium–SiC preforms could yield net-shape components with tunable thermal conductivity and expansion coefficients; CPS absorbed those process rights and built a proprietary near-net-shape forming and infiltration capability at Norton that has compounded into a defensible franchise. Where ceramic-based thermal-management peers such as Kyocera and Toshiba supply standardised packaging substrates, CPS positions around custom geometry. As Senior Scientist Mark Occhionero has noted: *"Our competition likes to sell one-size-fits-all. CPS designs products that specifically meet our customers' performance and design needs."* Copper base plates delaminate from ceramic substrates after roughly 4,000 thermal cycles; CPS AlSiC composites maintain thermal-dissipation integrity far beyond that threshold — a characteristic that becomes structurally important as SiC module lifetimes extend across EV drivetrain warranty horizons.

## Commercial Inflection: Record Revenue in Fiscal 2025

The demand shift registered sharply in the company's fiscal year ended December 2025. CPS reported revenue of **$32.6 million**, a 54 percent increase over fiscal 2024's approximately $21.2 million, and the strongest sales figure in the company's history. Gross margin recovered from negative territory — roughly negative one percent in fiscal 2024 — to approximately 16 percent for the full year and 14.6 percent in the fourth quarter alone. The company turned from a net loss of $3.1 million in fiscal 2024 to net income of $420,354 in fiscal 2025, reflecting the operating-leverage benefit of a fully ramped third production shift at Norton.

> "We closed 2025 with the strongest revenue in our Company's history, $32.6 million, an increase of 54% over 2024." — Brian Mackey, Q4 2025 earnings release, March 2026 ([CPS Technologies IR](https://cpstechnologysolutions.com/cps-fourth-quarter-financial-results/))

The quarter immediately preceding the frozen snapshot also produced a significant order-book event: a **$15.5 million follow-on contract** from a major multinational semiconductor manufacturer, representing approximately a 16.5 percent year-on-year increase in that customer's business, with deliveries scheduled over twelve months beginning October 2025. CPS closed an equity offering in October 2025 that raised net proceeds of **$9.5 million**, earmarked for general corporate purposes and a planned relocation to a larger advanced manufacturing facility — site evaluation was ongoing through Q1 2026. The company ended fiscal 2025 with a backlog of **$26 million**, largely scheduled to ship through 2026, plus $4.7 million in cash and $8.8 million in marketable securities against an undrawn $3.0 million credit facility.

## Defence Cluster: HybridTech Armor and Hermetic Packaging

HybridTech Armor®, CPS's metal-encapsulated ceramic composite panel, is qualified for installation as the strike face of advanced ballistic shields on US Navy CVN-class carriers, Marine Corps Assault Amphibious Vehicles, and Army UH-60 platforms. The product's saltwater and UV durability makes it attractive relative to polymer-matrix armour in maritime environments. Through mid-2024 the Navy's carrier programme was an active revenue contributor — a June 2023 follow-on order from Kinetic Protection, the Navy's armour prime, was valued at $1.4 million — but by Q1 fiscal 2026 management characterised HybridTech Armor revenue as "effectively zero," with new destroyer-programme contracts anticipated in the second half of 2026. A $100,000 Navy SBIR Phase 1 extension for Amphibious Combat Vehicle weight-reduction research was booked in Q1 2026, maintaining programme relationships ahead of a larger potential procurement cycle. Hermetic packaging for high-reliability avionics, GPS, and specialised integrated circuits provides the defence segment's more consistent revenue floor; management targets low-to-mid-30-percent gross margins on five-axis-machined hermetic components as new machining capacity comes online.

## Early 2026: Timing Noise and Structural Confidence

First-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $7.0 million fell slightly from $7.5 million a year earlier, compressing gross margin to 8.6 percent and producing a net loss of approximately $300,000. Management attributed the decline to order-timing phasing rather than demand erosion.

> "does not diminish our positive outlook for 2026, nor reflect a lack of orders or demand." — Brian Mackey, Q1 2026 earnings call, May 2026 ([Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/cps-technologies-q1-earnings-call-141450186.html))

A $4 million hermetic packaging order was booked after the quarter closed, with shipments expected to begin in Q2 2026. The company's end-market revenue mix between metal matrix composites and hermetic packaging oscillates — management described the split as "maybe 60-40, 70-30" — with SBIR funding contributing roughly five percent of revenue.

## Dossier Questions

The chapters that follow interrogate the structural durability of the FY2025 inflection. How concentrated is the $32.6 million revenue base — is the unnamed multinational semiconductor manufacturer the dominant contributor, and does that expose the backlog to a single customer's SiC module programme cycle? How does the Norton facility's existing footprint constrain volume beyond the $30-35 million range before the planned relocation completes, and on what timeline? Where does AlSiC fit relative to ceramics-based thermal solutions from Kyocera and Toshiba as SiC module designs evolve toward direct-bonded-copper and active-metal-brazed substrates? And how reliably does the Navy destroyer programme materialise in H2 2026 to replace the gap left by the carrier programme's pause?

chapters.title: From 1984 founding through Lanxide AlSiC commercialisation to the AI/EV inflection
chapters.body:
## Origins in Norton: A Materials Science Startup, 1984

CPS Technologies was incorporated in 1984 in Norton, Massachusetts, a small industrial town south of Boston that had long served as home to Saint-Gobain's abrasives operations and gave the company its geographic identity. The founding ambition was elemental: to translate laboratory-scale ceramic and composite materials science into manufacturable, commercially viable components. The company — originally named Ceramics Process Systems Corporation before adopting its current moniker — planted its flag at a moment when the advanced-materials sector was experiencing its first wave of serious industrial investment, driven by defence-procurement appetite for lightweight, high-performance structural and thermal materials.

Norton's early years were those of a classic materials-science venture: long gestation periods, modest revenue, and a business model built around process know-how rather than volume. The company's engineers worked with aluminium-based composites and ceramic systems, developing near-net-shape forming and infiltration techniques that would later become the manufacturing backbone of its commercial franchise. Revenue was thin and the customer base narrow; the company existed in the penumbra between research institution and production manufacturer. That positioning, though financially precarious, gave CPS a process-development fluency that few rivals could match.

## The Lanxide Inflection: AlSiC Arrives in the Mid-1990s

The pivotal chapter in CPS Technologies' history was written not in Norton but in Newark, Delaware, at the laboratories of Lanxide Corporation. Lanxide was, in the early 1990s, one of the most closely watched advanced-materials ventures in the United States, having developed a suite of proprietary infiltration and directed-metal-oxidation processes — marketed under the PRIMEX and DIMOX trade names — that allowed aluminium to be infiltrated into silicon carbide preforms under pressureless conditions. The resulting aluminium silicon carbide (AlSiC) composite combined the thermal conductivity of aluminium with the stiffness and, critically, the tunable coefficient of thermal expansion of silicon carbide, producing a material whose CTE could be dialled between roughly 7 and 12 parts per million per degree Celsius depending on the SiC volume fraction.

For power electronics packaging engineers, that tunability was transformative. Copper baseplates — the conventional substrate beneath IGBT and later SiC power modules — carry a CTE of approximately 17 ppm/°C, far above silicon's 3 ppm/°C and SiC's 4 ppm/°C. Repeated thermal cycling between those mismatched expansion rates cracks solder bonds and degrades module reliability. AlSiC at roughly 7–8 ppm/°C sits close enough to silicon and SiC to suppress that fatigue mechanism while delivering thermal conductivity of 170–200 W/m·K — superior to most ceramics used in comparable roles.

Lanxide's financial trajectory, however, did not match its technical ambitions. By the mid-1990s the company was navigating severe capital constraints, and it ultimately wound down its commercial operations. CPS Technologies moved to secure the intellectual property that Lanxide had assembled around pressureless metal infiltration, entering into a licensing and cross-licensing arrangement that gave Norton access to the core AlSiC process IP. That transaction, completed in the mid-1990s, was the hinge event in CPS Technologies' corporate history: it handed a small Massachusetts manufacturer the right to produce and sell AlSiC components to the global power electronics industry under a proprietary process that competitors could not easily replicate from first principles.

From that foundation CPS moved quickly to establish production capability at Norton, scaling the infiltration furnaces, binder systems, and near-net-shape forming lines needed to translate Lanxide's laboratory process into a repeatable manufacturing workflow. By the late 1990s the company was shipping AlSiC heat spreaders and baseplates to European and Japanese power-module manufacturers, establishing the customer relationships that would sustain the business through the following two decades.

## Two Decades of Specialty Franchise: Building the MMC Moat

The years between the late 1990s and the early 2020s were CPS Technologies' long middle passage — less dramatic than the Lanxide era, but the period in which the company built the durable competitive advantages that would later attract investor attention during the AI and EV demand inflections. Revenue ran in a range that SEC filings over the period placed broadly in the $20–30 million band annually, a scale modest by industrial standards but sufficient to sustain a profitable operation at Norton given the specialty nature of the product and the pricing power that came with it.

The commercial segment centred on power electronics thermal management. CPS supplied AlSiC baseplates and heat spreaders to manufacturers of high-power IGBT and, increasingly, SiC and GaN modules used in industrial drives, rail traction inverters, EV prototype programs, and RF power amplifiers. The customer list over this period included the major European and Japanese power semiconductor and module houses — companies whose module designs were engineered around CPS's specific AlSiC formulations and dimensional tolerances, creating switching costs that reinforced the franchise. Designing a competing baseplate solution into a certified module qualification takes years and hundreds of thousands of engineering hours; once CPS was designed into a platform, revenue tended to recur across the model's lifecycle.

Alongside the commercial business, CPS built a meaningful defence segment. HybridTec Armor — the company's branded aluminium-composite armour system — found a home in US Navy programmes as a lightweight alternative to steel for shipboard and vehicle applications. AlSiC's combination of low areal density, ballistic resistance, and corrosion tolerance made it attractive for naval environments where weight and maintenance intervals are critical programme parameters. The defence segment provided both revenue diversification and a degree of cyclicality insulation: armour and harsh-environment packaging programmes run on government contract timelines that diverge from commercial semiconductor cycles.

The company also supplied hermetic packaging for harsh-environment electronics — components exposed to extreme temperature swings, vibration, or corrosive atmospheres in military, space, and industrial applications. This product line reinforced CPS's reputation as a materials specialist capable of meeting stringent qualification standards, which in turn supported the pricing and margin profile of the defence segment relative to higher-volume commercial offerings.

Throughout this period, CPS Technologies was led by Grant Bennett, a long-tenured chief executive whose stewardship anchored the company's identity as a technically focused specialty-materials producer. Bennett's successor, Brian Mackey, who assumed the role of President and Chief Executive, inherited a franchise with established process IP, a proven customer base, and a manufacturing campus at Norton that had been refined over two decades of incremental investment.

## The AI/EV Inflection: 2020–2025

The structural demand shift that reshaped CPS Technologies' growth narrative arrived in overlapping waves beginning around 2020 and accelerating sharply through 2024–2025. The primary driver was the SiC power module transition in electric vehicles: as automotive OEMs and their Tier 1 power-electronics suppliers moved from silicon IGBT traction inverters to SiC-based designs — a shift that improved inverter efficiency by two to three percentage points and extended range — demand for AlSiC baseplates moved with it. SiC's lower CTE relative to silicon made the CTE-matching argument for AlSiC baseplates even more compelling in SiC module designs than it had been in IGBT applications, and the power-density increases involved raised thermal management requirements commensurately.

The second demand vector was AI infrastructure. The hyperscaler buildout of GPU-dense server racks through 2023–2025 drove rack-level power densities to levels — measured in tens of kilowatts per rack — that imposed new thermal management requirements on the power supply and conversion hardware within those installations. SiC and GaN power modules used in server power delivery units required baseplates and packaging substrates with thermal performance that CPS's AlSiC products were positioned to supply. The company characterised the dynamic in its investor communications as an AI server power module thermal demand inflection, and the phrasing captured the nature of the shift: not a gradual secular improvement but a step-change in the specification requirements arriving at its order desk.

To meet that demand, CPS Technologies undertook capacity scaling at Norton through 2024–2025, supported in part by equity capital raises. The fiscal year ending June — a legacy feature of the company's reporting calendar that differentiates it from calendar-year industrial peers — means that the full revenue impact of the inflection was spread across multiple reporting periods, complicating year-on-year comparisons but not obscuring the trajectory. Revenue mix was evolving: the commercial power-electronics segment was growing faster than the defence segment, altering the cyclicality profile of the business and increasing its correlation to semiconductor capital-expenditure cycles even as the defence anchor provided continuity.

From a 1984 founding through the Lanxide licence that gave it a proprietary material, across two decades of patient franchise-building, and into an inflection driven by the electrification of transport and the power demands of artificial intelligence, CPS Technologies arrived at the mid-2020s as a company whose small physical footprint in Norton, Massachusetts belied the structural importance of what it manufactured inside it.

chapters.title: AlSiC composites, heat spreaders, baseplates, armor, hermetic packaging
chapters.body:
The properties that make aluminum silicon carbide irreplaceable to a power-module designer are the same ones that make it difficult to manufacture at scale: a lattice structure that mimics the coefficient of thermal expansion of wide-bandgap semiconductors while conducting heat at rates approaching copper, all wrapped inside a rigid, machinable enclosure that survived tens of thousands of thermal cycles. CPS Technologies built its commercial franchise on mastering that contradiction over three decades at its Norton, Massachusetts campus.

## The AlSiC Material Platform

Aluminum silicon carbide is a metal matrix composite in which silicon carbide particles — typically comprising 50 to 70 percent of the structure by volume — are infiltrated with molten aluminum under carefully controlled pressure and temperature conditions. The resulting solid combined the thermal conductivity of the aluminum matrix, commonly in the range of 170 to 220 watts per meter-kelvin depending on SiC loading and infiltration parameters, with a coefficient of thermal expansion that could be tuned across a range of roughly 6.5 to 9 parts per million per degree Celsius by adjusting the SiC volume fraction.

That tunability was commercially decisive. Silicon carbide power semiconductors — the MOSFETs and diodes at the heart of EV traction inverters and AI server power stages — expanded and contracted at approximately 3.7 ppm/°C under thermal cycling. Copper, the conventional heat-spreader material, sat at 17 ppm/°C. The CTE mismatch between a copper baseplate and a silicon carbide die generated shear stress at the solder interface with every power cycle; over thousands of cycles, that stress propagated delamination cracks that eventually destroyed the module. An AlSiC baseplate tuned to 6.5–8 ppm/°C reduced the mismatch to a level the solder joint could tolerate across a module's service lifetime, converting what had been a reliability failure mode into a solved engineering problem.

CPS traced its AlSiC capability to the Lanxide Corporation technology lineage. Lanxide, a Newark, Delaware research company, developed pressureless metal infiltration and directed metal oxidation processes through the late 1980s and early 1990s — breakthrough techniques that could produce near-theoretical-density aluminum-ceramic composites without the high-pressure tooling costs of conventional powder metallurgy. When Lanxide encountered financial difficulties in the mid-1990s, CPS acquired rights to the relevant intellectual property and manufacturing know-how, establishing what became the company's core process franchise. By the mid-1990s the Norton campus had begun producing AlSiC components for early power electronics customers, and the company spent the following two decades building application-specific variants of the base technology across an expanding set of end markets.

## Heat Spreaders and Baseplates

The most commercially significant product families CPS manufactured were heat spreaders and baseplates for discrete power semiconductors and packaged power modules. A heat spreader is interposed between the semiconductor die and the cooling system — a liquid-cooled cold plate in automotive or server applications, or a finned air-cooled assembly in rail traction — to spread thermal load laterally and prevent hotspot formation. A baseplate served the additional function of structural substrate: the module's internal interconnects, ceramic isolation layers, and die stack were all bonded to the baseplate, which in turn mounted to the external cooling system.

For SiC-based power modules — now the dominant technology in EV traction inverters above roughly 100-kilowatt output — both functions demanded a material that CTE-matched the die stack, conducted heat aggressively, and tolerated the mechanical loads of automotive assembly. AlSiC satisfied all three constraints simultaneously while remaining lighter than the copper-molybdenum or copper-tungsten alternatives that predated the composite era. Weight was a secondary but nonzero consideration in EV powertrain design, where inverter mass compounded into range reduction at the vehicle level.

CPS manufactured these components to near-net-shape tolerances, meaning the as-infiltrated part required minimal post-processing to reach final dimensions. The process deposited liquid aluminum into a preformed SiC skeleton at controlled infiltration pressure, yielding a near-finished surface that could accept electroless nickel-phosphorus plating or gold flash directly — the plating layer serving as the bonding surface for die-attach solder or thermal interface material. Near-net-shape production reduced scrap rates relative to machined-from-billet alternatives and enabled the tight dimensional tolerances that power module assembly processes demanded.

## GaN RF Packaging Substrates

A parallel product line addressed gallium nitride RF power amplifiers used in defense radar, electronic warfare platforms, and — with growing commercial volumes — 5G base-station radio units. GaN-on-SiC RF power transistors generated high power density at microwave frequencies, but they required packaging substrates that could dissipate heat at the die footprint, maintain hermeticity under field conditions, and present the correct mechanical interface to the microwave circuit board.

AlSiC packaging housings served this application by providing a hermetically sealable enclosure with CTE close enough to GaN-on-SiC to survive the temperature swings of radar duty cycles. Defense procurement had driven this segment for years; CPS supplied custom-machined housings and lids that integrated with ceramic window frames and kovar seal rings to produce fully hermetic microwave packages. As GaN became the dominant technology for 5G massive-MIMO base stations, commercial demand for similar packaging architectures began supplementing the historically defense-weighted mix, broadening the addressable customer base for what had previously been a relatively narrow military specialty.

## HybridTec Armor

CPS Technologies marketed its naval composite armor under the HybridTec trade name — a family of aluminum-composite panel systems designed to defeat ballistic, blast, and fragmentation threats at weights significantly below steel equivalents. The US Navy represented the primary end customer, with HybridTec panels specified into hull and superstructure applications aboard surface combatants and support vessels where topside weight reduction directly affected stability margins and fuel economy over the service life of the hull.

The material architecture of HybridTec armor drew on the same MMC knowledge base as CPS's thermal products — aluminum matrix reinforced with ceramic particles — but optimized for dynamic energy absorption rather than thermal conduction. Unlike monolithic steel armor, the composite panel absorbed projectile energy through progressive ceramic fragmentation and aluminum matrix deformation, mechanisms that distributed impact energy over a larger volume of material and enabled the weight savings that naval architects sought in topside installations without compromising protection levels below those of the legacy steel systems they replaced.

Defense program timing created revenue lumpiness for the armor segment. Naval ship construction schedules, modification programs, and foreign military sales pipelines all introduced multi-year lag between program authorization and hardware delivery. CPS managed this variability by maintaining the armor segment as a complement to the more continuously-shipping commercial thermal management business, with defense programs providing revenue diversification and utilization fill rather than a second growth engine moving in lockstep with commercial cycles.

## Hermetic Packaging for Harsh Environments

Beyond RF packages, CPS produced a range of hermetic enclosures for electronics operating in undersea, downhole, and military avionic environments where moisture ingress and pressure differential would destroy conventional plastic-packaged circuits. Hermetic packages relied on the ability to seal aluminum or AlSiC housing bodies with metal lids using solder or weld bonds that maintained leak rates below specified thresholds across temperature cycling from cryogenic to elevated operating ranges.

The materials science challenge was that sealing dissimilar metals — aluminum or AlSiC housing bodies, kovar or Alloy 42 seal rings, borosilicate glass feedthroughs — required precisely matched CTEs at every interface across the full operating temperature envelope. CPS's materials expertise transferred directly to this problem: the same understanding of aluminum matrix composition and SiC reinforcement loading that yielded a target CTE for a power module baseplate could be applied to engineer a hermetic housing body whose expansion matched its seal-ring and feedthrough system, producing assemblies that met MIL-STD leak specifications over temperature.

## The 2024–2025 Power Module Inflection

The most consequential near-term demand driver visible through the frozen-window date of May 2026 was the acceleration in high-density power electronics for AI server infrastructure. Hyperscaler datacenter buildout through 2024 and into 2025 pushed rack-level power densities into ranges — 40-kilowatt racks giving way to 100-kilowatt and above configurations for GPU cluster deployments — that existing copper-based thermal management could not address without unacceptable cold-plate sizing constraints. Power module designers for server power supplies began specifying SiC switches in place of silicon at higher current densities, pulling demand for AlSiC baseplates from a customer segment that had historically relied on conventional materials.

EV traction inverter volume growth reinforced the same trajectory. As automotive OEMs and their tier-1 power electronics suppliers completed the transition from silicon IGBT to SiC MOSFET traction inverters through model-year 2024 and 2025 programs, AlSiC baseplate volumes scaled with unit output from plants in Europe, North America, and Asia. The two demand pools — AI infrastructure and EV traction — ran concurrently through 2024 and 2025, compressing what might otherwise have been a gradual ramp into a demand step-change that the Norton facility had to absorb while maintaining product quality and customer qualification timelines simultaneously.

CPS's competitive position in this environment rested on accumulated process experience — decades of refinement on the Lanxide-lineage infiltration process — and application-specific engineering capability for customer-specific geometries. Ceramic-based thermal management alternatives, including aluminum nitride and silicon nitride direct-bonded-copper substrates from competitors such as Kyocera and Rogers Corporation, addressed different layers of the packaging architecture. AlSiC baseplates occupied the base layer of the power module stack, underneath the ceramic isolation substrate, placing CPS in a position that was structurally complementary rather than directly competitive with ceramic substrate suppliers at the standard module architecture level — a differentiated niche that had proved durable across multiple technology cycles and appeared, through the frozen window, to be entering its most favorable demand environment in the company's history.

chapters.body:
## A Franchise Under Pressure, Then Rerouted

CPS Technologies entered fiscal 2022 as a quietly profitable specialty materials maker riding two parallel currents: a durable commercial franchise in aluminum silicon carbide thermal management, and a concentrated armor revenue stream from a U.S. Navy program. Over the four fiscal years ending December 2025, those currents moved in sharply opposing directions, producing first a peak, then a near-collapse, and finally the strongest top-line result in the company's four-decade history.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Gross Margin | Operating Income | Net Income |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $26.6M | 27.5% | $2.2M | $2.1M |
| FY2023 | $27.6M | 24.8% | $1.7M | $1.4M |
| FY2024 | $21.1M | (0.6%) | $(4.4M) | $(3.1M) |
| FY2025 | $32.6M | 16.2% | $0.4M | $0.4M |

*Sources: [CPSH FY2025 10-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000814676/000143774926006687/cpsh20251227_10k.htm); [CPSH FY2024 10-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000814676/000143774925008029/cpsh20241228_10k.htm); [StockTitan CPSH Financials](https://www.stocktitan.net/financials/CPSH/)*

The FY2022–FY2023 period represented the franchise at its historical best. Revenue edged to $27.6 million in fiscal 2023, a 3.8% advance on 2022's $26.6 million, while gross margins held near 25 percent. Operating income of $1.7 million in 2023 reflected a business that had absorbed the pandemic trough of $20.9 million in 2020 and rebuilt cleanly — a modest but consistent machine whose Norton, Massachusetts campus operated profitably on long-cycle defense deliveries supplemented by growing commercial thermal-management volumes.

## The Anatomy of the FY2024 Trough

Fiscal 2024 brought a dual shock that erased three years of earned margin. The first blow was qualitative: quality issues with a major commercial customer late in 2023 forced the redirection of production resources toward corrective action, compressing output and margins in the first quarter of 2024. The second blow was structural: the HybridTec Armor® contract with Kinetic Protection — the prime contractor supplying composite armor panels for U.S. Navy vessels — reached completion during the second quarter of 2024. That contract had underpinned a substantial portion of CPS's defense revenue; its end removed what amounted to a recurring, relatively high-margin volume floor.

The quarterly sequence tells the collapse in granular terms. First-quarter 2024 revenue came in at $5.9 million as quality-remediation work consumed capacity. The second quarter fell further to $5.0 million, against $7.4 million in the year-earlier period, as armor shipments wound down. The third quarter of 2024 was the nadir: revenue of $4.2 million against $6.3 million a year prior, with gross margin swinging to negative 12 percent as fixed manufacturing costs ran against a skeleton volume base. Operating loss for the quarter reached $1.5 million.

The economics of a fixed-cost specialty ceramics operation impose a stark asymmetry: contribution from every incremental unit is high, but the unabsorbed burden of kilns, forming presses, and skilled labor is severe when volume thins. At $4.2 million of quarterly revenue — roughly 60 percent of the run-rate from twelve months earlier — the Norton facility was essentially covering variable input costs and nothing else.

CPS's response was operational rather than financial. In late August 2024, management activated a third production shift, accepting near-term cost drag from training alongside existing workers. President and chief executive Brian Mackey acknowledged the transition cost plainly in the third-quarter 2024 earnings statement: the new staff "worked alongside other workers for training, impacting overall cost of goods sold." He nevertheless flagged a turning point: "We are optimistic about significantly improved performance in the fourth quarter and beyond."

The fourth quarter of 2024 bore out that confidence in a limited sense. Revenue rebounded 40 percent sequentially to $5.9 million — equal to the first quarter of the year — as the third shift moved from training to production. Mackey described the mechanism directly: "Revenue rose 40% sequentially from the third quarter, due in large measure to an added third shift and increased production capacity." Gross margin remained in negative territory at -5.1 percent, but the direction had changed. Full-year 2024 closed at $21.1 million in revenue with a gross loss of $118,638 and an operating loss of $4.4 million.

## Commercial Scale and the Semiconductor OEM Anchor

The structural rebuilding of the commercial revenue base had begun quietly, in parallel with the armor-related disruption. In October 2024, CPS disclosed a $12 million contract with "a major, longstanding multinational semiconductor manufacturer based overseas" to deliver power module components over a twelve-month period beginning that month. The components — AlSiC baseplates and packaging substrates — were destined for traction inverters in high-speed rail, wind turbine converters, and electric and hybrid vehicles. Mackey described the award as "noteworthy growth in our core business of aluminum silicon carbide products," emphasising the company's commitment to "the growing needs of our client and its customers, particularly in the green energy, automotive and transportation fields."

That contract effectively replaced the armor revenue structurally, if not all at once. When the October 2024 intake began flowing through production in earnest — combined with the three-shift capacity — the commercial channel scaled rapidly. First-quarter fiscal 2025, ending March 2025, produced $7.5 million of revenue, a record at the time, up 27 percent year-over-year. Gross margin recovered to 16.4 percent, operating income turned positive at $0.1 million, and CPS returned to net profitability after a four-quarter lapse.

The momentum compounded through the year. By the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, quarterly revenue reached $8.2 million — another record — pushing full-year 2025 to $32.6 million, a 54 percent advance on 2024's depressed base. The headline represented the highest annual revenue in the company's history, and Mackey's year-end commentary struck a tone of earned relief: "we closed 2025 with the strongest revenue in our Company's history…marking a great comeback for CPS."

## End-Market Mix: Replacing Armor with Commercial Depth

CPS does not formally segment revenue between commercial and defense lines in its public disclosures. However, the narrative assembled from quarterly filings and contract announcements makes the directional shift legible. Through fiscal 2022–2023, the business operated with a meaningful defense component — HybridTec Armor deliveries contributed consistently, alongside hermetic packaging for harsh-environment electronics, DOE-funded development contracts, and NAVAIR prototyping awards. The armor program's completion in mid-2024 compressed the defense share materially.

Management's stated goal — "to fully replace its armor contract with revenue from other products" — was achieved by the time the fourth-quarter 2024 results were released. The replacement mechanism was primarily the semiconductor OEM power-module relationship and a broadening of commercial thermal-management customers. Three new Army Phase I SBIR contracts totalling $750,000 were awarded in the first quarter of 2025, and a Phase II Department of Energy contract for $1.1 million was disclosed in the third quarter of 2024, alongside a $200,000 NAVAIR development award. These maintained a defence-adjacent presence without re-establishing a large single-program dependency.

The anchor on the commercial side was reaffirmed dramatically in October 2025, when CPS announced a $15.5 million follow-on contract with the same undisclosed multinational semiconductor manufacturer, covering a further twelve months from October 2025 through September 2026. The contract represented a 16.5 percent year-over-year volume expansion from the same customer — and, by arithmetic, confirmed that the October 2024 contract had delivered approximately $13.3 million in revenue during its execution period. Applications remained centered on high-speed rail, energy grid infrastructure, and mobility. Mackey framed the renewal in explicitly industrial terms: "This expanded engagement with a globally respected partner underscores the rising demand we're seeing across the industrial, energy, and mobility sectors."

## Operating Leverage: Margin Recovery and Its Ceiling

The gross margin recovery from -0.6 percent in fiscal 2024 to 16.2 percent in fiscal 2025 was driven overwhelmingly by volume absorption rather than pricing gains. At the Norton campus, fixed manufacturing overhead — depreciation, shift-supervisory labor, facility costs — is largely invariant to quarterly output levels. When revenue scaled from a $4–6 million quarterly run-rate to a $7–8 million run-rate, those costs were spread across meaningfully more units, compressing cost-per-part and restoring positive gross contribution.

The 2022 benchmark of 27.5 percent gross margin illustrates the ceiling: at that revenue level and that product mix, the Norton facility ran with comfortable overhead absorption. The 16.2 percent achieved in fiscal 2025 reflects a business still climbing toward that operating point — higher gold pass-through pricing also inflated the revenue denominator without improving margin proportionally, as precious-metal content in hermetic packaging is recognized at cost-plus with minimal margin contribution. Stripping gold pass-through from the revenue base would likely show a somewhat stronger underlying margin recovery.

## Capital Structure: The October 2025 Equity Raise

The FY2024 operating loss of $4.4 million drew down the balance sheet meaningfully. Cash and equivalents fell from approximately $8.8 million at the beginning of the fiscal year to $3.3 million by December 2024, a consumption of more than $5 million as the company funded losses and working capital needs with existing liquidity. Total assets stood at $18.9 million against stockholders' equity of $14.5 million at the end of fiscal 2024 — a modest but adequate buffer for a company with no significant debt and a manufacturing asset base that was not encumbered.

The equity market provided the capacity reset. In October 2025, CPS closed a public offering of 3,450,000 shares of common stock — including the underwriter's full over-allotment option — at $3.00 per share, generating gross proceeds of approximately $10.35 million and net proceeds of $9.54 million. Roth Capital Partners acted as sole book-running manager. The intended use of proceeds encompassed general working capital, capital expenditures, and — critically — the expansion of production capacity, with management simultaneously disclosing that it was "evaluating potential sites for a larger, advanced CPS manufacturing facility" with a transition targeted during calendar 2026.

The offering left CPS in a materially stronger liquidity position than the prior year-end. By December 2025, the company held $4.5 million in cash and $8.8 million in marketable securities — combined liquid assets of $13.3 million — against total current assets of $24.8 million. Shares outstanding after the offering stood at 17,991,780, an increase of roughly 24 percent from the pre-offering base, a dilution that management implicitly accepted as the price of funding capacity ahead of the $15.5 million contract and prospective facility transition.

## Working Capital and the Path Forward

Working capital dynamics at CPS reflect the lumpy, program-driven nature of specialty composites manufacturing. Receivables and inventory move with contract cadence rather than on smooth seasonal curves; the $12 million semiconductor OEM contract in October 2024 required raw-material inventory build and labor staffing ahead of revenue recognition. The working capital draw through late 2024 was partly responsible for the cash decline beyond the operating losses alone.

The fiscal 2025 recovery generated positive, if modest, operating cash flow, with the improved income supplemented by working capital normalization as the backlog-to-delivery cycle stabilized. Management's articulation of a new facility strategy — supported by the October 2025 equity proceeds — sets the next capital allocation question: transition costs, lease obligations, and equipment transfers for a manufacturing relocation are material one-time items for a company of CPS's scale. The positioning, as Mackey described it in early 2026, anticipated "strong revenue, continued margin expansion" as the precondition for absorbing that transition cost. The $15.5 million semiconductor OEM commitment running through September 2026 provides at least twelve months of revenue visibility against which to execute that move.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## Setting the Multiple Baseline

Assigning precise valuation multiples to CPS Technologies requires working from a range of inputs rather than a single anchored figure. With approximately 15.6 million diluted shares outstanding — derived from the most recent 10-Q and DEF 14A filings available on [SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=CPSH) — and a twelve-month trading range running roughly from $3.50 to $7.50 on NASDAQ, the implied market capitalisation spans $55 million to $117 million. This chapter reasons from a mid-range reference price near $5.50 per share, yielding a market cap of approximately $86 million; readers requiring precision should verify against NASDAQ pricing data as of 23 May 2026. The company carried a modest net-cash position in recent quarters with minimal long-term debt drawn, leaving enterprise value broadly in line with equity value — call it $82–88 million for working purposes.

Against the revenue base, that pricing implies an EV/Sales multiple of approximately 2.4x on a trailing-twelve-months basis if revenue is running near $34–36 million — a plausible range given the AI-server and EV traction inverter demand inflection visible through fiscal 2025 filings. On a forward basis, if consensus revenue growth towards $40–42 million for fiscal year ending June 2026 proves achievable, EV/Sales compresses to roughly 2.0–2.1x. For a specialty materials company with structural differentiation, that sits meaningfully above the sector median but below the premium commanded by pure-play semiconductor materials names. At the margin-line, EBITDA has historically been thin: prior-cycle CPS operated at low-to-mid single-digit percentage EBITDA margins, meaning that even at $3–4 million of EBITDA, the implied EV/EBITDA multiple reaches 20–28x — elevated, and justified only if operating leverage is genuinely inflecting. If the scaling thesis delivers EBITDA margins in the 12–15% range on a $40 million revenue base, the forward EV/EBITDA drops toward 14–18x, which begins to look defensible against specialty materials peers. Price-to-book is largely uninformative for an asset-light-ish manufacturer with modest tangible book, but on the basis of reported equity of roughly $25–30 million, current pricing implies a P/B of around 3x — confirming that the stock embeds a meaningful growth premium above replacement cost.

## Historical Re-rating in Context

CPS Technologies spent much of the 2018–2022 period trading at EV/Sales multiples of 0.5x to 1.2x, reflecting its positioning as a stable-but-slow specialty MMC manufacturer with revenue in the $20–25 million range and earnings near breakeven in softer years. The company rarely attracted meaningful institutional sponsorship, and its micro-cap liquidity constrained the multiple ceiling. The re-rating that began in late 2022 and accelerated through 2023–2024 tracked the broader SiC/GaN power module investment cycle: as Wolfspeed, Infineon, and STMicroelectronics disclosed multi-billion-dollar capacity expansions for silicon carbide devices used in EV inverters and AI server power supplies, investors reached for the thermal-management supply chain. CPS, as a near-sole-source AlSiC baseplate and heat-spreader supplier to that module ecosystem, received a corresponding multiple expansion — at times trading above $7 and implying EV/Sales above 3x. That premium proved fragile when the EV demand cycle softened in late 2024 and SiC module makers trimmed near-term production guidance. The stock pulled back toward the $4–5 range through early 2026, representing a partial de-rating but one that still leaves valuation well above the pre-2022 trough, reflecting the market's belief — not yet retracted — that secular demand for AlSiC thermal management is structurally higher than it was before the AI infrastructure buildout began.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

The most instructive comparison group combines direct materials-technology peers serving power electronics with broader specialty materials companies sharing CPS's dual commercial-defense revenue mix.

| Company | Ticker | EV/Sales (NTM) | EV/EBITDA (NTM) | P/E (NTM) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPS Technologies | CPSH | ~2.0–2.4x | ~18–26x | NM/elevated | Micro-cap; AI/EV growth premium |
| Rogers Corporation | ROG | ~1.5–1.8x | ~12–15x | ~18–22x | Power electronics substrates; ~$900M revenue |
| Materion Corporation | MTRN | ~0.7–0.9x | ~11–14x | ~16–20x | Specialty alloys; ~$1.4B revenue |
| UFP Technologies | UFPT | ~1.2–1.5x | ~13–16x | ~22–26x | Specialty composites; defense/medical mix |
| GrafTech International | EAF | ~1.0–1.3x | ~9–12x | NM | Graphite electrodes; cyclical; useful floor |
| Cohu Inc | COHU | ~1.4–1.7x | ~14–18x | ~20–25x | Semi test/packaging; adjacent supply chain |

CPS trades at a premium to all named peers on EV/Sales, which is defensible only if its revenue growth rate materially exceeds the group and its AlSiC near-net-shape process represents durable pricing power rather than commodity commodity-adjacent manufacturing. Rogers is the most instructive anchor: it serves overlapping power electronics customers with copper-clad laminates and advanced substrate solutions, trades at a meaningful discount to CPS on both EV/Sales and EV/EBITDA, and carries a substantially larger revenue base that provides more visibility. The gap suggests either that CPS warrants a small-cap growth premium or that it is simply more thinly traded and therefore noisier in its multiple. Materion's deeper discount reflects both scale and commodity-ier product mix; UFP's closer alignment reflects comparable end-market diversity. On any rigorous normalised basis, CPS's current multiple prices in an optimistic growth scenario — not a base case.

## Intrinsic-Value Framing

A simplified DCF illuminates what the current price is actually embedding. Discounting at a 12% WACC (appropriate for a micro-cap with customer concentration, thin liquidity, and binary program risk), and assuming a modest terminal-growth rate of 3%, the present value of a business generating $5 million of free cash flow — roughly consistent with a $40 million revenue base and 12–13% FCF conversion — yields an intrinsic value around $42–50 million, or roughly $2.75–$3.20 per share. To justify the mid-range $5.50 reference price under the same discount framework, the model requires either: FCF of $8–10 million within three to four years (implying $55–65 million of revenue at sustained 15%+ FCF margins), or a lower discount rate that bets on de-risking via multi-year take-or-pay contracts that have not yet been publicly disclosed. Neither is implausible, but neither is baked into confirmed guidance. The gap between model intrinsic value and current market price is the AI/EV option value the stock is carrying — and it is material.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $9.00–$11.00 per share.** Revenue reaches $48–52 million by fiscal 2027 as hyperscaler AI server power density drives AlSiC baseplate volume beyond prior capacity constraints, and the US Navy armor programme delivers a multi-year committed tranche. Operating leverage on the Norton campus pushes EBITDA margins to 18–20%, generating $9–10 million of EBITDA. At 14x forward EV/EBITDA — a multiple Rogers commanded at its 2021 peak — enterprise value reaches $126–140 million and equity value per share lands in the $9–11 range. This scenario requires the SiC/GaN volume ramp to hold through 2026–2027 and at least one large new customer win on the commercial side.

**Base case — $5.00–$6.50 per share.** Revenue grows to $38–42 million in fiscal 2026 and $44–48 million in fiscal 2027, consistent with observed booking trends and customer programme timelines. EBITDA margins stabilise in the 12–14% range. At 16x forward EV/EBITDA the enterprise value is $82–105 million, roughly in line with the current reference price. The stock neither re-rates further nor collapses; it grinds with the growth. This is the scenario in which the narrative is correct but the upside is already substantially discounted.

**Bear case — $2.25–$3.25 per share.** EV and AI capital expenditure cycles slow materially through 2026 — not a remote risk given Federal Reserve policy uncertainty and hyperscaler capex volatility — and SiC module producers return to inventory digestion as occurred in 2024. Revenue growth stalls around $30–33 million, EBITDA compresses to $2–3 million, and the stock re-rates toward its pre-AI trough multiple of 8–10x EV/EBITDA. A secondary equity raise to fund partially idled capacity would further dilute existing holders. At 9x $2.5 million EBITDA the enterprise value is $22–25 million; adding back net cash and dividing by the diluted share count returns a price near $2.50.

| Scenario | Revenue (FY2027E) | EBITDA Margin | EV/EBITDA | Price Target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | $48–52M | 18–20% | 14x | $9–11 |
| Base | $44–48M | 12–14% | 16x | $5–6.50 |
| Bear | $30–33M | 6–8% | 9x | $2.25–3.25 |

## What the Market Is Pricing In

At roughly $5.50, the market is paying for something between the base and the low end of the bull: it assumes the secular demand thesis is real, that AlSiC retains its thermal-management advantage over competing ceramic substrates, and that CPS can sustain operating leverage into a modestly higher revenue run-rate without significant dilutive capital raises. What it is not pricing in — and this is the dossier's central tension — is execution risk at a company that has historically run lean on both headcount and capital, has not publicly disclosed take-or-pay agreements with its largest customers, and competes in a supply chain increasingly targeted by larger Asian materials incumbents willing to invest in AlSiC process capability. The consensus read appears to be that CPS deserves a growth multiple but not a compounder multiple; the dossier's read is that the gap between those two depends almost entirely on whether the company converts the 2024–2026 demand inflection into durable, multi-year customer programme commitments before a cyclical correction tests the thesis. Until those commitments are disclosed with enough specificity to underwrite the FCF model, the current valuation is more sentiment than earnings power — which makes it both more volatile and more interesting than its micro-cap positioning suggests.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through AI/EV demand inflection and Navy program timing
chapters.body:
## The Setup: A Specialty-Materials Company at a Demand Crossroads

When CPS Technologies reported its fiscal 2022 results, the Norton, Massachusetts manufacturer occupied a well-worn market position: a profitable but modestly sized supplier of aluminum silicon carbide metal matrix composites, serving a stable base of power-electronics customers who valued the material's thermomechanical properties and a U.S. government defense sector that intermittently valued its armor. Revenue ran in the low-to-mid twenty-million-dollar range — enough to sustain operations and protect the franchise, not enough to attract the attention of most institutional investors. The company's NASDAQ ticker, CPSH, traded with the thin volume of a deeply specialist name that only its customers and a handful of small-cap materials analysts could readily identify.

What the 2022 numbers did not yet reflect was that two secular demand curves — one driven by artificial intelligence infrastructure, one by the electrification of mobility — were beginning to accelerate in precisely the direction of CPS's core product line. AlSiC baseplates and heat spreaders are not interchangeable commodities; they are precision-machined components that sit directly beneath silicon carbide power semiconductors, managing the thermal interface between increasingly dense SiC and GaN switching die and the module housings around them. As those die shrank, switched faster, and ran hotter, the thermal management specification tightened — and AlSiC's combination of near-matched coefficient of thermal expansion with copper-tungsten-like conductivity became harder for module designers to substitute away from.

## FY2023: The Signal Starts to Distinguish Itself from the Noise

Through the first half of calendar 2023, management began describing a demand environment that differed qualitatively from prior cycles. President and CEO Brian Mackey, who had navigated the company through an earlier period of military armor contract variability and the post-COVID supply-chain disruption, told investors on multiple quarterly calls that commercial bookings were running ahead of historical patterns, with power-electronics customers — chiefly the power-module manufacturers supplying silicon carbide devices into data-center and industrial applications — placing larger and longer-dated purchase orders than the company had previously seen from that segment.

The mechanism was straightforward even if the magnitude was not yet clear: the proliferation of large-language-model training and inference infrastructure, anchored by hyperscaler capex cycles, drove demand for high-density server power supply units. Those PSUs increasingly specified SiC-based power-factor-correction and DC-DC converter stages, which in turn required the kind of thermally capable, CTE-matched baseplates that CPS had been manufacturing since the Lanxide licensing era. Each AI-optimized rack represented multiple power modules; each data center represented thousands of racks. The math, if the volume materialized, was meaningful for a company with a revenue base measured in the tens of millions.

On the EV side, the traction-inverter segment was generating a parallel demand signal. The global automotive OEM community had committed to SiC-based inverter platforms across multiple vehicle programs, and the tier-one module makers supplying those inverters — drawing on substrate supply from Wolfspeed, onsemi, STMicroelectronics, and Infineon — were qualifying AlSiC baseplates for production. CPS's role as a domestic, specification-qualified supplier gave it a structural position in that qualification chain that would be difficult to displace once locked in.

## The Navy Timing Problem and the Quarter-to-Quarter Noise

Against the commercial tailwind, the defense revenue line continued to behave as it always had: unpredictably. CPS Technologies has held positions on multiple U.S. Navy programs — including vehicle armor and armor for individual protection applications using AlSiC-based materials — but government procurement timelines rarely align with the fiscal quarters of a public company. Delivery schedules slip, continuing resolutions delay appropriations, and program office priorities shift in ways opaque to outside observers.

The result, visible across the 2022–2025 reporting period, was a persistent source of quarterly noise. In periods when armor deliveries clustered into a quarter, defense revenue would spike and total company margins would widen, since armor contracts tend to carry better gross margins than high-volume commercial heat-spreader production. In intervening quarters, the defense line could fall sharply, compressing blended margins even as commercial volume grew. Mackey and his team were consistent in characterizing this as timing rather than demand — the programs remained funded, the qualification positions remained intact — but the lumpiness complicated any attempt to read a clean sequential trend line into the quarterly data.

| Period | Commercial Dynamic | Defense Dynamic | Key Management Theme |
|--------|-------------------|-----------------|---------------------|
| FY2022 | Stable; early AI signal emerging | Armor deliveries intermittent | Foundational demand intact |
| FY2023 | Accelerating; AI/EV bookings building | Program timing delays visible | Backlog growth; capacity watching |
| FY2024 | Meaningful revenue inflection | Armor deliveries uneven; Navy program schedule scrutiny | Capacity investment; equity raise |
| FY2025 | AI demand sustained; EV mix maturing | Navy timing remains program-dependent | Execution and margin management |

## FY2024: Capacity Becomes the Binding Constraint

By the time CPS Technologies was reporting through fiscal 2024, the commercial demand signal had become sufficiently large that the question shifted from whether the demand was real to whether Norton could produce enough product to capture it. The facility, which occupies a campus in Norton with roots in the Lanxide-era AlSiC licensing arrangement, has a fixed physical footprint and a manufacturing process that involves powder metallurgy steps — infiltration, machining, and inspection — that cannot be compressed indefinitely without capital investment and workforce additions.

Management acknowledged on earnings calls that lead times had extended and that the company was evaluating capacity expansion options. An equity raise — structured to avoid excessive dilution while funding the capital program — became part of the financial narrative. For a company of CPS's size, even a modest primary offering represents a meaningful balance-sheet event; the decision to access the equity markets rather than lever the balance sheet reflected both the capital intensity of the expansion and management's conservatism around debt in a business with some degree of program-timing cyclicality.

The capacity conversation intersected directly with customer qualification cycles. SiC module manufacturers operate on qualification timelines measured in months, not weeks; getting approved on a new baseplate platform requires thermal cycling tests, reliability qualification to automotive or IEC standards, and sign-off across multiple engineering functions. Customers that had begun qualifying CPS product in 2022 and 2023 were, by 2024, reaching the point of ramp-ready production release. The compounding of multiple simultaneous ramp events — AI power modules, EV traction inverters, and legacy industrial markets — created a demand-supply tension that management had not navigated at this scale before.

## FY2025: Execution Under Scrutiny

Entering fiscal 2025, the demand picture remained favorable in aggregate but more complex in detail. AI-infrastructure investment by hyperscalers did not taper as some analysts had modeled; the buildout of inference-optimized capacity extended the procurement cycle well beyond the initial training-cluster phase. Power-module suppliers continued to call on CPS for baseplate supply, and the company's domestic-supplier positioning carried additional value as customers sought to reduce single-source exposure to Asian material suppliers in a period of elevated geopolitical uncertainty.

EV demand proved more uneven. The broader automotive market slowed its electrification pace from earlier projections, and several OEM programs that had anchored AlSiC baseplate forecasts revised their production schedules. The net effect was that EV-related commercial revenue grew less linearly than the AI-related revenue, introducing a new source of quarterly variability to complement the perennial Navy timing problem.

Mackey's commentary through the 2025 reporting period emphasized operational execution — yield rates at Norton, throughput per square foot of manufacturing floor, and the maturation of the expanded capacity added in 2024. The company was no longer arguing that it deserved a premium valuation because demand was building; it was being asked to demonstrate that it could convert that demand into durable earnings power. Gross margin trajectory became the primary metric on which investor patience would be measured as the fiscal year progressed toward the frozen-snapshot date of late May 2026.

## What the Cadence Reveals

The four-year arc from fiscal 2022 through the 2025 reporting period illuminates a company at a classic specialty-materials inflection point: a proprietary process, a defensible market position, and a demand environment finally large enough to test whether the manufacturing operation can scale without sacrificing the precision-quality standards that justified the franchise in the first place. Quarterly results will continue to be noisy — the Navy will deliver armor on the Navy's schedule, and power-module customers will adjust orders in response to their own inventory cycles — but the secular direction of the demand curve, anchored in the thermomechanical realities of SiC switching physics, is not in dispute. The question CPS Technologies is answering, quarter by quarter, is whether Norton can grow at the pace the market is prepared to reward.

chapters.title: Brian Mackey, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## The Bennett Inheritance

Grant Bennett joined CPS Technologies in November 1985, barely a year after the company's 1984 founding in Norton, Massachusetts, as vice president of sales and marketing. He had come from Bain & Company, the Boston consulting firm, and carried with him an undergraduate degree from the University of Utah and a graduate degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The composite-materials shop he walked into was still a research-intensive startup; his job was to make it a company. Seven years later, in September 1992, the board elevated him to president, chief executive officer, and treasurer — a triple designation that reflected both the organisation's small scale and the degree to which its institutional knowledge had consolidated around one individual.

The tenure that followed lasted twenty-nine years. Across that span Bennett presided over the commercialisation of aluminum silicon carbide under the cross-licence framework established with Lanxide Corporation in the mid-1990s, the progressive accumulation of power-electronics and defence customers, and several near-misses with operating losses during cyclical downturns. He served simultaneously as the company's most credible technical narrator, its longest-tenured outside salesman, and its de facto investor-relations director — roles that blurred naturally at a company whose annual revenues rarely exceeded $25 million. His retirement, effective 1 July 2021, was the first true succession event in the organisation's history.

Before departing he signalled confidence in his successor with characteristic understatement:

> "Michael McCormack has my complete support and confidence."

Bennett remained on the board, and by the time of the April 2026 annual meeting was chairing the compensation and nominating committee — keeping the company's longest institutional memory anchored inside governance three decades after he first joined.

## The McCormack Interregnum

McCormack joined CPS in January 2021 as chief operating officer, recruited for what the board described as a track record in aerospace and defence sector technology firms and an ability to "generate organic growth in a technology-based manufacturing company." When Bennett stepped down six months later, McCormack was promoted to the top seat. His tenure tracked a post-pandemic demand recovery that drove revenues to new highs, and the company credited him with operational improvements during a period of rising customer interest in AlSiC for silicon-carbide power modules.

The run ended without warning on 21 April 2023. McCormack submitted his resignation; the company disclosed that the departure was "not a result of any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to the Company's operations, policies or practices." He had held the office for fewer than two years.

Charles K. Griffith Jr., the chief financial officer, stepped into an acting-president role while the board conducted a search — carrying both functions for roughly four months, through what proved to be an active period of customer engagement. His willingness to absorb the dual burden prevented an operational vacuum at a moment when the SiC/GaN power module demand cycle was beginning to accelerate.

## Brian Mackey: West Point, Wharton, Norton

The board settled on Brian Mackey in the summer of 2023. His appointment as president and chief executive officer became effective 14 August 2023, and his biography stood apart from that of every CPS chief executive before him.

Mackey graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point in 1991 with a B.S. in engineering, then served as an officer in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers at Fort Bragg, North Carolina — a formation that has contributed disproportionately to the pool of manufacturing-company leaders who can execute in resource-constrained, programme-driven environments. He returned to civilian education in the late 1990s, earning an MBA from the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School before re-entering industry.

His commercial career traced a path through precision-engineered machinery and advanced materials. At Synchrony, a developer of magnetic bearing systems for high-speed rotating machinery, he joined as chief operating officer; when Dresser-Rand acquired the company in 2012 he transitioned to general manager of the Synchrony business unit within the combined Dresser-Rand/Siemens organisation. The role gave him extended experience at the intersection of precision engineering and large-programme customer management — a profile closely analogous to CPS's defence and power-electronics franchise.

Immediately before joining CPS, Mackey served for approximately five years as chief executive of Engi-Mat Co. in Lexington, Kentucky, a developer of metal oxide and ceramic nanomaterials. Under his direction the company became a volume supplier on a U.S. Navy Program of Record and won significant research contracts from the Department of Defense and the Department of Energy. The parallels to CPS's own defence-composite exposure were deliberate.

Board chairman Francis Hughes, welcoming the appointment, described Mackey as bringing "the vision, expertise, and leadership to further unlock the tremendous capabilities of the senior management team and all CPS employees," citing specifically his industrial background in advanced materials and electromechanical assemblies and his aerospace and defence customer knowledge.

In October 2025, Mackey filed a Form 4 disclosing the open-market purchase of 16,500 shares of common stock at $3.00 per share, lifting his total reported beneficial ownership to 36,500 shares. The transaction was executed at the same price as the underwritten public offering that CPS closed that month — a 3,000,000-share deal at $3.00, with Roth Capital Partners acting as sole book-runner, that raised approximately $9.5 million in net proceeds earmarked for a manufacturing-facility relocation intended to nearly double usable floor space. Mackey's concurrent purchase alongside public investors was a transparent alignment signal.

By the year's end he had delivered the company's highest-ever annual revenue:

> "As expected, we closed 2025 with the strongest revenue in our Company's history, $32.6 million, an increase in revenue of 54% over 2024, marking a great comeback for CPS as we position the organisation for the future."

His total reported compensation for fiscal 2025 was $505,162 — a base salary of $319,125, a cash bonus of $151,994, and option awards valued at $21,278. A subsequent grant of 10,000 option shares in May 2026 at an exercise price of $4.67, vesting ratably from 2027 through 2030, reflected the board's view that the chief executive's long-cycle incentive remained modest relative to the demand tailwinds confronting the business.

## CFO Transition and the Operating Bench

Griffith had served as CPS's chief financial officer since April 2019. He held an accounting degree from the College of William and Mary and an MBA from Bryant University, and had spent twenty-seven years as vice president of finance at Vertex Distribution before stints at SPRI Clinical Trials Global. His institutional knowledge spanned nearly all of CPS's most recent commercial transition. Management acknowledged his exit with characteristic brevity: "Chuck has been an integral part of CPS's growth and success over the past seven years."

His successor, Chris Fraser, joined CPS on 4 May 2026 and formally assumed the chief financial officer title on 18 May 2026. Fraser arrived from Precision Castparts — the Berkshire Hathaway aerospace-castings subsidiary — where he had served as controller overseeing financial operations across three aluminium casting plants. Prior roles included chief financial officer positions at federal-grant- and SBIR-funded early-stage ventures and senior finance positions at A.W. Chesterton and Oxford Instruments America. Fraser qualified as a chartered accountant through Deloitte in London and holds a B.S. in economics from the University of Warwick — a European-trained finance background that deepened the team's manufacturing-process cost credibility.

The wider operating leadership included Daniel Barton as vice president of operations, a retired Army officer and OIF III veteran with more than thirty years of manufacturing and supply-chain management experience, and Stephen Kachur, Ph.D., as vice president of technology. Kachur, a Carnegie Mellon materials scientist who earned his doctorate there after an undergraduate degree from Lehigh University, had researched ceramic matrix composites and additive manufacturing for aerospace and hypersonic applications — technical depth that reinforced CPS's credibility with defence customers pushing into next-generation composite programmes.

## The Board

At the close of the April 2026 annual meeting, the board comprised five independent directors under Nasdaq standards.

| Director | Title | Key Background | Director Since |
|---|---|---|---|
| I. James Cavoli | Chairman (from April 2026) | President, Swagelok Co. (2021–2024); COO from 2020; Army captain; Ford Motor Co.; Progressive Insurance; founder LS Insights | December 2024 |
| Francis J. Hughes Jr. | Director; former Chairman | President, American Research & Development Corp. (VC) since 1992; B.S./M.S. MIT; MBA Harvard Business School | 1993 |
| Grant C. Bennett | Director; Comp/Nom Chair | President & CEO, CPS Technologies 1992–2021; prior Bain & Company; M.S. MIT, B.A. Utah | 1992 |
| Ralph M. Norwood | Director; Audit Chair | CPS CFO 2011–2019; founder Navigator Advisors; former CFO SatCon Technology; 20+ years VP Finance, Polaroid; CPA; Army veteran | 2019 |
| Daniel C. Snow, Ph.D. | Director | Director of MBA Programs, BYU Marriott School; visiting faculty Harvard Business School and Tuck; prior Ford financial analyst | 2008 |

Cavoli's December 2024 appointment and subsequent elevation to chairman represented the most meaningful governance refresh in several years. Hughes, welcoming him to the board, had noted that Cavoli brought "a broad array of relevant skills and experiences that will help the board guide the company forward" — a formulation that pointed toward the operational and scaling challenges ahead as AlSiC demand from power-module customers grew faster than CPS's Norton floor space could comfortably absorb.

Norwood, as audit committee chair and the board's designated audit-committee financial expert, brought a layered credibility: he had spent eight years as CPS's own chief financial officer before joining the board in 2019, meaning the company's outside overseer of financial reporting had a granular understanding of its cost structure, inventory practices, and capital requirements. Snow's academic specialisation in strategy and competitive dynamics at a business school anchored in manufacturing-intensive industries offered a complementary lens.

The board's compensation structure followed a small-cap industrial template: annual cash retainers supplemented by stock-option grants, with the company adopting an explicit hedging prohibition covering all directors and officers. The April 2026 proxy also carried a proposal — approved by shareholders — to increase the company's authorised common shares from 20 million to 25 million, providing headroom for further equity incentives, potential capital raises, and opportunistic acquisitions as the facility-expansion cycle matured.
