chapters.title: Power module customers, EV tier-1s, US Navy, RF/defense electronics
chapters.body:
## The AlSiC Baseplate as Critical Thermal Infrastructure

For most of the power electronics supply chain, the baseplate is invisible — a slab of metal tucked beneath silicon carbide dies, its function taken for granted until thermal failure exposes the inadequacy of a cheaper substitute. CPS Technologies built its commercial franchise on that invisibility, spending three decades making aluminum silicon carbide components that module manufacturers specified into designs without public acknowledgment and rarely changed once qualified. By the mid-2020s, however, the architecture of power electronics had shifted in ways that made CPS's narrow specialty considerably more visible: AI server power supplies, EV traction inverters, and GaN radio-frequency amplifiers all converged on higher junction temperatures, tighter thermal budgets, and coefficient-of-thermal-expansion (CTE) constraints that AlSiC satisfied and copper or standard aluminum did not.

The structural case rested on physics. SiC power devices operated at junction temperatures approaching 175°C, compared with roughly 150°C for silicon IGBT predecessors, and the switch from silicon to SiC carbide die shrank the CTE mismatch tolerance at the die-attach interface. AlSiC — with thermal conductivity in the 160–200 W/m·K range and a CTE of approximately 7–9 ppm/°C — occupied a narrow material window that aluminum (CTE ≈ 23 ppm/°C) could not reach and that ceramics-based alternatives such as AlN or Si₃N₄ met at higher cost and with inferior machinability for large-area baseplates. CPS's near-net-shape pressure infiltration process, commercialized through cross-licenses from Lanxide Corporation's legacy intellectual property in the mid-1990s, allowed it to produce complex geometries with embedded features at margins that a ceramics shop could not replicate.

## Power Module Customers: Named Exposure and Structural Undisclosure

CPS Technologies did not publicly name its power module manufacturing customers in routine filings through the frozen window, a contractual norm common among specialty materials suppliers embedded in qualified supply chains. What the company's annual reports to the [Securities and Exchange Commission](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=CPSH&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40) did disclose, consistently, was the degree of concentration: a small cohort of customers typically accounted for the majority of revenue, with the two or three largest individually above the ten-percent disclosure threshold. That concentration cut both ways — it gave CPS reliable volume visibility against long-qualification-cycle customers who found switching costs prohibitive, while exposing the company's revenue line to any single customer's inventory cycle.

The broader roster of AlSiC baseplate consumers in the global power module industry provided context for who CPS's unnamed accounts most plausibly were. Infineon Technologies, the world's largest power semiconductor company by revenue, had for years incorporated AlSiC baseplates across its IGBT and SiC module families — the CoolSiC and PrimePACK lines among them — as standard thermal architecture for high-power-density applications above roughly 100 amperes. Mitsubishi Electric's power module division, a dominant supplier to rail traction and industrial drives markets in Japan and globally, sourced AlSiC baseplates for its NX-series and comparable high-reliability lines. STMicroelectronics and ON Semiconductor, both accelerating SiC module shipments for automotive and industrial applications through 2024 and 2025, represented incremental demand pools as SiC displaced silicon IGBT in new designs. Wolfspeed, the pure-play SiC substrate and device company, supplied wafers and bare die into third-party module assemblers, some of whom sourced their own baseplates; others bought finished modules incorporating AlSiC from packagers who were themselves CPS customers.

The AI server acceleration that became visible in hyperscaler capital-expenditure data from late 2023 onward created a new demand vector that CPS's management characterized as a meaningful inflection. AI server power supplies — the 48V bus converters and intermediate bus architectures inside GPU server racks — used high-frequency SiC and GaN switching stages that operated at elevated power densities. As rack power climbed from 10 kilowatts toward 100 kilowatts and beyond in the generational step from NVIDIA H100 to B200 and beyond, the thermal management spec tightened commensurately, pulling AlSiC substrates into configurations where copper had previously been accepted.

## EV Tier-1s and the Traction Inverter Migration

The EV traction inverter represented the largest single incremental market opportunity CPS articulated through the 2024–2026 period. A 800-volt silicon carbide traction inverter in a premium battery-electric vehicle contained between six and twelve SiC power modules, each requiring a precision baseplate whose CTE matched the SiC die and whose thermal resistance budget sat within the system's junction-to-coolant spec. As the global automotive industry committed to SiC inverters — driven by range and efficiency demands that silicon IGBT could not meet at 800-volt bus voltages — demand for AlSiC baseplates scaled proportionally with module shipment volumes.

The EV power electronics tier-1 supply chain that sourced or embedded AlSiC substrates included companies such as BorgWarner, Continental Automotive, and Vitesco Technologies, each of which manufactured power inverter assemblies for OEM customers. Japanese and Korean module specialists — Denso, Rohm, and others — participated in parallel supply chains feeding Asian OEM platforms. CPS's customer relationships in automotive ran through these module and inverter assemblers rather than directly through automakers, insulating the company from direct OEM program volatility while exposing it to the assemblers' own qualification and ramp timelines.

The qualification cycle for automotive-grade power module materials ran eighteen to thirty-six months from engineering sample to production release, which meant that design wins being converted to revenue through 2024 and 2025 reflected customer commitments made in 2022 and 2023, near the peak of EV build-out optimism. The subsequent moderation in EV volume growth across several Western OEM platforms in 2024 introduced timing risk into CPS's revenue ramp, though the secular shift from silicon IGBT to SiC across virtually all new inverter platforms sustained the per-unit AlSiC content even as absolute volume projections were revised.

## US Navy and Defense Armor

CPS's defense franchise operated on a separate cadence from its commercial electronics business, structured around program continuity and government procurement cycles rather than design-win qualification timelines. The company's HybridTec Armor system — a composite armor architecture incorporating AlSiC and related metal matrix materials — had been in use on US Navy surface vessels and amphibious platforms for an extended period, providing ballistic and blast protection at weights that conventional steel solutions could not match at equivalent protection levels.

Navy armor programs provided CPS with a recurring revenue base that partially offset commercial cycle volatility, though program size and timing were subject to defense appropriations and shipyard schedules that introduced their own lumpiness. The company also supplied hermetic electronic packaging components for defense and aerospace customers — housings, lids, and substrate frames for radar, electronic warfare, and communications modules that required hermeticity and dimensional stability across wide temperature ranges. These packaging components served defense primes and their Tier-2 electronics manufacturing subcontractors, and while individually smaller than the power module baseplate business, they represented a stable, high-specification niche where CPS's infiltration process produced geometries that machined aluminum or brazed ceramics could not replicate economically.

## GaN RF and Military Electronics Substrates

Gallium nitride RF power amplifiers — the enabling technology for phased-array radar, electronic warfare, and next-generation communications — required thermal substrate solutions capable of handling local heat flux densities substantially higher than those in power conversion modules. GaN-on-SiC devices, widely used in defense RF applications, operated at power densities exceeding 10 W/mm² at the die level, creating baseplate and carrier requirements that AlSiC met through its combination of high thermal conductivity and CTE compatibility with SiC carrier wafers.

CPS served this market through direct supply to defense electronics manufacturers and through module assemblers who incorporated its substrates into completed RF front-end assemblies. The customer base overlapped with the broader US defense electronics industrial base — primes and sub-primes involved in radar, signals intelligence, and directed-energy programs — and benefited from the sustained growth in phased-array and active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar procurement across US military services and allied customers.

## Norton Campus: Capacity Scaling Against Demand

All of CPS Technologies' production ran through a single manufacturing campus in Norton, Massachusetts, a configuration that concentrated operating leverage in one facility while limiting geographic redundancy. The Norton site housed the company's pressure infiltration furnaces, machining cells, and quality inspection lines, and capacity expansion at Norton was the primary capital allocation question the company faced as commercial and defense demand simultaneously pressed against existing throughput.

Management commentary through 2024 and into 2025 addressed capacity investment in the context of the AI server and EV SiC demand inflection — the company undertook capital expenditure to add infiltration capacity and expand machining throughput, funded in part through the operating cash flow that the commercial demand surge generated. The single-site concentration remained both a strength, in terms of process control and institutional knowledge density, and a risk, in terms of any disruption at Norton having immediate revenue consequences with no fallback manufacturing option.

| End-Market Cluster | Primary Product | Key Demand Driver (through 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| AI server power supplies | AlSiC baseplates / substrates | Hyperscaler CapEx, rack power density |
| EV traction inverters | AlSiC baseplates | SiC module adoption at 800V platforms |
| Rail and industrial drives | AlSiC baseplates | Electrification and efficiency mandates |
| US Navy armor | HybridTec Armor panels | Vessel protection programs |
| Defense RF / radar | AlSiC substrates, hermetic packaging | GaN AESA radar build-out |
| Harsh-environment electronics | Hermetic packages | Defense and aerospace program mix |

The customer base CPS had assembled — geographically dispersed across US, European, and Asian power module manufacturers, anchored by long-qualified relationships in defense, and exposed to three structurally distinct demand cycles — gave the company an unusual diversification profile for a manufacturer with under $30 million in annual revenue. What it did not give the company was pricing power commensurate with its technical differentiation: AlSiC baseplates remained contract-priced, typically on multi-year supply agreements, with annual volume and pricing adjusted at renewal. The operating leverage that Norton's fixed-cost base offered was therefore accessible only if volume grew — a condition that the 2024–2025 AI and EV inflection appeared, at least temporarily, to satisfy.

chapters.title: Where CPSH sits against Kyocera, Toshiba, ceramics-based thermal management peers
chapters.body:
## A layered stack, not a head-to-head fight

The instinct in industrial equity research was to set CPS Technologies against Kyocera and Toshiba on a single axis and ask which ceramics franchise had the better hand. The architecture of a silicon-carbide or gallium-nitride power module made that framing misleading. Inside a modern traction inverter or grid-tied converter, the semiconductor die sat atop a direct-bonded copper (DBC) ceramic substrate — aluminium nitride or silicon nitride — which provided electrical isolation and lateral heat spreading. That substrate was then bonded to a baseplate, typically aluminium silicon carbide (AlSiC), which carried the mechanical load and shuttled heat into a liquid-cooled cold plate beneath. Kyocera, Toshiba Materials, NGK Insulators and the former Rogers curamik unit (acquired by Advanced Energy Industries in 2022) competed in the substrate layer. CPS Technologies competed in the baseplate layer below it. The two were stacked together inside the same module; they were complements far more than they were substitutes.

That distinction set the tone for everything that followed in the competitive analysis. A Kyocera AlN substrate did not displace a CPS AlSiC baseplate any more than a copper trace displaced a silicon die. The peer set that actually constrained CPS's pricing power and market share lived one layer down, among the small handful of firms that could metal-matrix-cast AlSiC at production scale — and that list was strikingly short.

## The baseplate physics that boxed copper out

The case for AlSiC began with a coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) problem that copper could not solve. Silicon carbide die expanded at roughly 4 ppm/K; AlN and Si₃N₄ DBC substrates sat near 4–5 ppm/K. A copper baseplate expanded at 17 ppm/K. Each thermal cycle therefore pulled the solder joint between substrate and baseplate in opposite directions, and after roughly 4,000 cycles — the kind of duty seen by an EV inverter over a decade of stop-start driving — fatigue cracks propagated through the solder layer and the module failed. CPS claimed AlSiC delivered "more than two times longer module life" against a copper-baseplate reference, a number consistent with the underlying CTE mismatch arithmetic.

The alternatives that did solve the CTE problem — copper-molybdenum (CuMo) and copper-tungsten (CuW) — solved it at the cost of weight. Where AlSiC weighed 2.89–3.01 g/cm³, CuMo and CuW came in at 10–17 g/cm³, three to six times heavier. For an aerospace customer specifying a satellite payload, or an automotive OEM trimming unsprung mass from a drive unit, that penalty was disqualifying.

| Baseplate Material | Thermal Conductivity (W/m·K) | CTE (ppm/K) | Density (g/cm³) | Relative Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AlSiC (CPS) | 180–200 | 7–8 | 2.89–3.01 | Medium |
| Copper | ~400 | 17 | 8.96 | Low |
| CuMo | ~180 | 6–8 | 10–17 | High |
| CuW | 170–200 | 5–8 | 16–17 | Very High |

The AlSiC CTE figure of 7–8 ppm/K sat close enough to the AlN substrate above it that the laminated stack moved as a single body under thermal load. That was the physical basis on which CPS's product had displaced copper inside high-reliability modules; it was also the reason ceramic substrate makers and CPS appeared together on bills of materials rather than against each other.

## Kyocera, Toshiba, NGK and Rogers — adjacent, not opposing

Kyocera held roughly 22% of global high-purity AlN substrate capacity in 2025, with output exceeding 250,000 units a year and total company revenue north of $15 billion across its broader ceramics and electronics portfolio [Next Move Strategy Consulting](https://www.nextmsc.com/report/aluminum-nitride-ain-substrate-market-mc4511). Toshiba Materials specialised in silicon nitride substrates — thermal conductivity of 70–90 W/m·K, flexural strength of 700–900 MPa and a CTE of 3.2 ppm/K — which had become the preferred substrate for automotive traction inverters because of their resistance to harsh thermal cycling. NGK Insulators ran AlN and Si₃N₄ ceramic lines at scale, and Rogers curamik, now folded into Advanced Energy Industries, supplied DBC on alumina, AlN and Al₂O₃.

None of these companies produced AlSiC baseplates. They sold the layer above. To the extent CPS shared customer relationships with them, the relationship was symbiotic: a Tier-1 power-module assembler buying Kyocera AlN often bought CPS AlSiC to bond beneath it. The competitive risk from that quartet was indirect — a substrate maker pushing for vertical integration downward, or specifying a CuMo baseplate to a captive customer — rather than head-on.

## The actual direct competitor: Denka

The peer that mattered most was Denka, the Japanese chemical group whose ALSINK product line expanded by roughly 2,000 metric tons of AlSiC capacity in 2023 and reported thermal conductivity above 200 W/m·K. CPS's own 10-K identified the rivalry in unambiguous terms: "CPS's primary direct competitor in MMCs is Denka, a large Japanese chemical company" [CPSH 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000814676/000143774926006687/cpsh20251227_10k.htm). Denka's parent had multi-billion-dollar revenue and a chemical-industry balance sheet that dwarfed CPS's $32.6 million top line.

Despite that asymmetry, CPS had not been relegated to margin-player status. The company's April 2025 annual general meeting presentation estimated that its annual shipment volume represented approximately 25% of the near-term available AlSiC market — a figure that, if accurate, made it Denka's only consequential global peer, with the two incumbents splitting the market and leaving little oxygen for a third entrant.

The 10-K added an important commercial boundary condition: copper remained viable where power levels were low enough. "In low voltage applications, a copper solution is sufficient as the heat being generated is not enough to degrade the reliability of the power module. As voltage levels and the heat related to them go up, MMC baseplates become the preferred solution." That boundary was migrating — SiC and GaN devices operated at higher voltages and switching frequencies than the silicon IGBTs they replaced, systematically expanding the addressable AlSiC territory at copper's expense.

A second tier of Chinese MMC producers offered lower prices but, in the company's own words, were "generally not yet able to provide the delivery, performance, quality and reliability required by the market." DWA Aluminum Composites, a US peer focused on aerospace and defence MMCs, overlapped on materials but rarely on the same baseplate sockets. That was the full direct-competitor universe.

## Hermetic packaging and armour: different fights, different moats

CPS's hermetic packaging segment lived in what the 10-K described as a "highly fragmented" market populated by Egide of France, the AMETEK Engineered Interconnect & Packaging division of the $6 billion-plus NYSE-listed parent, and Qnnect, the former Hermetic Solutions Group. CPS's stated differentiator was narrow but defensible: it was the only producer of hermetic packages with AlSiC bases, a combination that mattered for space and defence applications where weight, thermal match and hermeticity were jointly specified. The Mars Perseverance rover and the MethaneSAT satellite carried CPS hardware as proof points of that heritage.

The armour business sat in a different category again. The 10-K's competition section stated its position with deliberate plainness:

> CPS has no direct competitors for its armor solution. Rather competition is based on three factors, effectiveness, weight and price... We believe our armor solution provides significant advantages regarding its effectiveness per pound, hence the reason it was selected by the US Navy for the crew served weapons stations on its air craft carrier fleet.

The broader ceramic-armour landscape included CoorsTek and Saint-Gobain's ceramic-armour franchise in adjacent composite-armour applications, but neither had penetrated the naval HybridTec specification niche. CPS and its commercialisation partner Kinetic Protection were pursuing contracts for additional Navy ship classes, described in the April 2025 investor presentation as "opportunities which represent a multiple of the CVN order." The HybridTec programme had completed its initial aircraft-carrier delivery by the snapshot date and no firm follow-on backlog had been publicly disclosed, making the segment episodically lumpy in the near term despite the longer-horizon pipeline.

## The qualification clock as the real moat

The most underappreciated competitive feature was not material chemistry but the sales cycle. The 10-K disclosed that a CPS baseplate sale "usually begins at the design stage of customers" and typically required "three to four years" from first engagement to production revenue. The filing described a representative case where the company "worked closely with a customer for over two years in the prototyping and development phase, after which the completed module entered into its one to two year qualification phase at the automotive OEM." Once qualified, programmes "last for many years" — and switching suppliers meant restarting the clock.

That dynamic was visible in management's commentary on the Asian pipeline: CPS reported "positive meetings with potential major baseplate customers in Japan and China who are moving forward with qualification of CPS baseplates." Each such qualification, if completed, locked in a multi-year revenue annuity that a price-cutting Chinese entrant could not dislodge without offering its own multi-year qualification timeline first.

## Process know-how without patent walls

Underneath the qualification moat sat a more technical one. CPS's QuickCast pressure infiltration process produced near-net-shape parts from SiC preforms; its QuickSet injection-moulding line ran above 55 vol% solids loading, used sublimation debinding, held sintered tolerances of ±0.2%, and pushed thousands of parts a week off the line without final machining. The CFO put it plainly:

> It's difficult to make, which means it's really hard for competitors to get into this market.

Crucially, the core processes were not patent-protected in the traditional sense. They sat behind trade secrecy and accumulated process know-how — the same posture that had kept high-end specialty-materials firms defensible long after their original patents lapsed. The company reported eight US patents in force as of December 2025, with international counterparts, but described its proprietary processes as the primary vehicle of competitive differentiation.

## Scale asymmetry, and the constraint that mattered

The honest weakness was scale. CPS booked $32.6 million in FY2025 revenue, a record and a 54% jump from $21.1 million in FY2024, against AMETEK at $6 billion-plus, Kyocera above $15 billion, and Denka with multi-billion-dollar chemical revenue behind it. The 10-K conceded the company had "fewer resources than some competitors" and that larger rivals "may develop more advanced products or reduce prices."

A second, underappreciated structural exposure sat in trade policy. CPS exported MMC baseplates into the European Union duty-free. The annual report flagged the vulnerability directly: "If a European manufacturer begins producing similar products, import duties could be imposed, increasing costs for our EU customers and potentially reducing demand for our products." Given that significant European revenue was tied to traction-inverter programmes in the Siemens and ABB-ecosystem customer base, a European AlSiC entrant — or a regulatory shift — could reorder competitive economics in that market without touching product quality.

The mitigant on scale was that CPS was production-constrained, not demand-constrained. The company evaluated a new and larger manufacturing facility for 2026 to relieve the bottleneck. Customer concentration remained high — the top three customers accounted for 64% of FY2025 revenue — but that concentration was the mirror image of the qualification moat: programmes large enough to dominate a $32 million revenue base were programmes where switching costs were correspondingly enormous. Set against an AlSiC end-market that [Fortune Business Insights](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/aluminum-silicon-carbide-market-109500) sized at $302 million in 2024 and projected to reach $1.36 billion by 2034 at a 16.2% CAGR — with power electronics and semiconductor packaging at roughly 38% of demand in 2025 — the binding question for CPSH was not whether Kyocera would crush it. It was whether CPS could pour enough AlSiC fast enough to hold its estimated 25% of the available market as Denka added capacity and Chinese manufacturers closed the quality gap.

---

chapters.title: Timeline from 1984 founding through AI/EV demand inflection
chapters.body:
## Origins at Norton: The 1984 Founding

CPS Technologies was incorporated in Norton, Massachusetts in 1984 with a mandate that was straightforward to state and devilishly difficult to execute: manufacture metal matrix composite materials — alloys in which a metallic matrix is reinforced by ceramic particulates — at a cost and quality level that real industrial customers would buy. The company occupied a modest manufacturing campus in Norton that would, over the subsequent four decades, become the single-site production base for what evolved into one of the world's most specialised aluminum silicon carbide franchises. In its early years, the company worked to develop near-net-shape forming and pressurised metal infiltration processes, proprietary techniques that would eventually allow it to produce AlSiC components with the dimensional precision and microstructural consistency that power electronics packaging demands.

The materials science underpinning CPS's eventual niche was well established in academic literature by the early 1980s: silicon carbide particulates, when infiltrated with aluminium, yield a composite whose coefficient of thermal expansion can be tuned to match silicon semiconductors far more closely than aluminium alone — a property critical for power module reliability across thousands of thermal cycles. What was not established was a commercially viable manufacturing route, and that gap defined the company's first decade.

## The Lanxide Cross-License and AlSiC Commercialisation

The pivotal structural moment in CPS Technologies' early history came through its licensing and cross-licensing arrangements with Lanxide Corporation, the Newark, Delaware materials pioneer that had spent the 1980s developing a broad portfolio of ceramic and metal matrix composite synthesis techniques. [CPS Technologies IR](https://www.cpstechnologysolutions.com/investors) By the mid-1990s, Lanxide's AlSiC intellectual property — covering pressurised infiltration processes central to economical AlSiC production — had been licensed into CPS's manufacturing framework. The arrangement gave CPS access to process chemistry that compressed what might otherwise have been another decade of development, and it positioned the Norton facility to begin volume supply of AlSiC heat spreaders and baseplates to power electronics assemblers at a moment when insulated gate bipolar transistor modules were beginning their commercial ramp across industrial drives and rail traction applications.

Lanxide itself would eventually wind down its commercial operations in the late 1990s, a casualty of the capital intensity of scale-up and the cyclicality of early advanced-materials markets. CPS, operating with a narrower product scope and a more capital-efficient near-net-shape process, survived and consolidated position as one of very few Western producers capable of volume AlSiC supply to power module assemblers.

## Building the Franchise: Two Decades of Specialty MMC

Through the late 1990s and into the 2000s, CPS Technologies built what amounted to a quietly durable specialty-materials franchise. Its customer base centred on power semiconductor module assemblers — the companies that package discrete IGBT and diode chips into the hermetic, thermally managed modules used in motor drives, rail traction inverters, and utility-scale power conversion equipment. AlSiC baseplates, bonded directly beneath the ceramic direct-bonded-copper substrates carrying the semiconductor chips, provided both the mechanical base of the module and the primary thermal expansion matching layer. Losing that layer to an inferior material risked delamination and field failure; the switching cost for a validated production line was consequently high, cementing CPS into qualified supplier positions that proved durable across multiple product generations.

Grant Bennett, who served as the company's chief executive through much of this formative stretch, presided over a business that remained intentionally narrow — Norton-only manufacturing, a single core material system, and a deliberately small headcount that kept fixed costs contained. Revenue scaled incrementally through the 2000s and into the 2010s, typically ranging within a band of roughly $20–30 million, a scale that reflected the niche character of the AlSiC market rather than any failure of commercial execution. [SEC EDGAR CPSH filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=CPSH&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)

## Defense and Navy: HybridTec Armor Programs

Parallel to its power electronics franchise, CPS developed a second revenue stream in defence composite materials. The company's HybridTec Armor product line applied AlSiC's combination of hardness, low areal density, and resistance to ballistic penetration to naval and military vehicle protection programmes. The US Navy became a recurring customer, drawing on CPS's Norton facility for armour panels that offered weight advantages over legacy ceramic-faced systems — a meaningful attribute on surface combatants where topside weight drives stability margins. The defence segment introduced programme-timing variability into CPS's revenue cadence: large armour delivery orders could produce lumpy quarterly results, and programme continuation was subject to procurement cycles and budget authorisations outside the company's control. Nonetheless, the Navy relationship provided a strategic second axis to the business, insulating CPS from full dependence on the commercial power electronics cycle.

## Brian Mackey and the Transition to AI/EV Demand

Brian Mackey assumed the role of President and Chief Executive Officer and guided the company into the structural demand shift that began materialising in earnest through 2024 and 2025. The proximate driver on the commercial side was the convergence of two independent electrification megatrends — AI server infrastructure and electric vehicle traction — onto the same SiC and GaN power module supply chain that CPS had served with IGBT-era baseplates and heat spreaders for two decades.

The mechanism was thermal: wide-bandgap semiconductors, principally silicon carbide, switch at higher frequencies and tolerate higher junction temperatures than silicon IGBTs, but they also concentrate more thermal flux through a smaller die area. As hyperscaler buildout of AI training and inference clusters drove rack-level power density beyond 10 kilowatts and then toward 30–50 kilowatts per rack, the power supply and power conversion modules feeding those racks required thermal management substrates capable of handling the increased heat flux while maintaining dimensional stability across thousands of thermal cycles. AlSiC's CTE match to SiC — the new substrate of choice for high-density power conversion — made CPS's baseplates and heat spreaders structurally advantaged.

Simultaneously, the ramp of SiC-based traction inverters in electric vehicle platforms — driven by OEM programmes at the major automotive tier-1 power electronics suppliers — replicated the same thermal management requirement at automotive production volumes. EV traction inverters operating at 800-volt bus architectures and switching at frequencies above 20 kilohertz impose a thermal cycling profile on baseplates that further reinforces the material-selection case for AlSiC over aluminium.

## Forward Catalysts: Capacity, Customers, and the Next Phase

The demand inflection through 2024–2025 surfaced two near-term capacity questions for the Norton campus. First, whether existing forming and infiltration capacity could be debottlenecked and expanded quickly enough to capture the commercial backlog building across AI power module and EV SiC module customer programmes without triggering extended lead-time penalties. Second, whether incremental equity capital — the company undertook financing activity through 2024–2025 to support capacity investment — would prove sufficient relative to the scale of the opportunity or require further raises. [CPS Technologies IR](https://www.cpstechnologysolutions.com/investors)

GaN RF power amplifier packaging, serving both defence electronics modernisation programmes and commercial 5G/6G base station infrastructure, represented a third commercial vector with distinct customer and procurement characteristics from the AI and EV streams, providing some demand diversification. Additional Navy and defence armour programme awards, should they materialise through the 2026 procurement cycle, would contribute further to the non-commercial revenue base.

For a company that spent the better part of four decades as a $20–30 million specialty-materials niche player, the convergence of AI, EV, and defence demand onto its precise material system — at a moment when Western AlSiC supply alternatives are limited — constituted a structural inflection that management was navigating with the same operational conservatism that had characterised the Norton facility since 1984.

chapters.title: AlSiC process IP, Lanxide legacy, near-net-shape forming, defense armor IP
chapters.body:
## The Lanxide Inheritance

CPS Technologies built its intellectual-property foundation on a piece of corporate history that most investors had long since forgotten. Lanxide Corporation, the Newark, Delaware materials pioneer, spent much of the 1980s and early 1990s developing novel routes to ceramic and metal matrix composites — processes that could infiltrate a porous silicon carbide preform with molten aluminum and yield a dimensionally stable, thermally conductive part at a fraction of the energy cost of traditional powder-metallurgy routes. When Lanxide's commercial ambitions outran its capital and the company restructured through the mid-1990s, its process IP did not vanish. CPS Technologies — already several years into its own aluminum-based materials work from its 1984 founding in Norton, Massachusetts — secured license and cross-license rights to the Lanxide AlSiC portfolio, acquiring the technical scaffolding it would build upon for the next three decades.

The Lanxide legacy covered two broad categories of know-how: directed-infiltration chemistry and near-net-shape preform engineering. The former described conditions under which molten aluminum, under controlled atmosphere and temperature, would spontaneously or pressure-assistedly penetrate a silicon carbide particle bed without catastrophic oxidation or reaction; the latter described how that preform could be shaped before infiltration so the finished composite required minimal secondary machining. Both capabilities were, and remained, central to CPS's commercial proposition.

## Pressure Infiltration and Near-Net-Shape Forming

The pressure infiltration process that CPS operated at Norton was, at its core, a materials engineering problem of unusual precision. A green preform — silicon carbide particles or fibers arranged in a tool to approximate the final part geometry — was loaded into a pressure vessel, surrounded by molten aluminum alloy, and subjected to elevated isostatic pressure sufficient to drive the metal into pore spaces too narrow for spontaneous capillary action. The resulting composite carried SiC volume fractions typically in the range of 55–70 percent, yielding coefficients of thermal expansion between 6 and 9 parts per million per degree Celsius — closely matched to the gallium nitride and silicon carbide dies mounted above, whose mismatch-induced stresses had long been the dominant failure mode in high-power electronics packaging.

Near-net-shape capability translated directly into economics. A baseplate or heat spreader that emerged from the pressure-infiltration cycle within tolerances close enough to the finished drawing could skip several grinding and lapping operations, compressing lead times and lowering scrap rates. CPS's process engineers refined the tooling geometries and the particle-size distributions of the SiC charge over years of production, accumulating process recipes that constituted trade secrets distinct from the underlying Lanxide patents — and, as those foundational patents aged into the public domain, increasingly the primary competitive barrier the company could defend.

The company's 10-K filings noted that CPS held both patents covering specific AlSiC compositions and process parameters and a body of proprietary know-how embedded in the operational procedures and institutional memory of its Norton facility. The combination — formal IP plus the tacit knowledge required to execute consistently at commercial volumes — created an entry barrier that competitors attempting to replicate AlSiC infiltration at the same dimensional tolerances found costly to cross. CPS did not disclose the precise count of active patents in its annual reports, but framed its competitive moat in terms of this dual structure: documented IP plus manufacturing know-how accumulated over decades of customer-specific qualification runs.

## HybridTec Armor and the Defense Composite Franchise

The same infiltration process that produced thermal management substrates for SiC power modules served a categorically different market when the product geometry shifted to armor panels. CPS's HybridTec Armor program applied aluminum-infiltrated ceramic composite structures to naval applications, where the trade-off between areal density and ballistic protection was acute. Composite armor built around silicon carbide tiles or fiber preforms encapsulated in a ductile metal matrix offered defeat mechanisms — ceramic comminution, metal plastic deformation, and energy redistribution — that traditional rolled homogeneous armor steel could not replicate at equivalent areal weight.

HybridTec Armor targeted United States Navy surface vessel and submarine programs, positioning CPS as a specialty supplier within a defense industrial base that valued qualified, domestic sources for advanced materials. The company's infiltration process, already proven in high-volume thermal management production, adapted to armor geometries with modifications to preform architecture and the alloy chemistry of the infiltrant. The resulting panels required the same process discipline — controlled atmosphere, precise thermal cycling, validated tooling — that CPS had institutionalized for electronics packaging customers, and the production infrastructure overlapped meaningfully.

Defense armor contracts carried their own IP implications. Development work performed under government contracts was subject to federal acquisition regulations governing data rights and government purpose license grants, meaning the government retained certain rights to use CPS-developed technical data in specified circumstances. CPS's filings acknowledged this framework without characterizing it as a material constraint on commercialization, reflecting a standard feature of small-scale defense materials contracting rather than a company-specific exposure.

## Trade Secrets as the Durable Moat

By the mid-2020s, the formal patent position CPS inherited and extended had matured alongside the underlying Lanxide-era filings. What remained — and what management consistently cited as the firm's durable competitive position — was the combination of process recipes tuned to specific customer qualification requirements, workforce expertise embedded in Norton's technical staff, and the qualification history itself. A new customer qualifying a power module manufacturer's baseplate needed not just technical capability from its supplier but documented process control records, failure analysis data, and the engineering relationship required to iterate on part geometry across product generations. That history could not be purchased off the shelf and accumulated slowly.

The result was a franchise that was less patent-thicket than process-fortress: an accumulation of know-how, customer-specific qualification data, and manufacturing institutional memory that had compounded since the Lanxide license was consummated. As SiC and GaN power module designs pushed junction temperatures higher and thermal interface budgets tighter through 2024 and 2025, the value of a supplier capable of delivering qualified AlSiC substrates at tight dimensional tolerances — and of iterating on composition and geometry in close engineering partnership with module designers — only increased.

chapters.title: Customer concentration, end-market cyclicality, defense program timing, scale, governance, competitive
chapters.body:
## Customer Concentration

CPS Technologies' commercial book rested on a narrow roster of power-semiconductor and module manufacturers whose own fortunes rose and fell with the capital-expenditure cycles of hyperscalers, automotive OEMs, and defence procurement offices. By the 2024–2025 period, the company's heat-spreader and baseplate shipments were concentrated among a handful of SiC and GaN power-module makers—names that analysts mapped to Infineon Technologies, STMicroelectronics, Wolfspeed, ON Semiconductor, and Mitsubishi Electric, among others—each of which was simultaneously navigating its own customer-concentration dynamic with the EV and AI server markets. CPS disclosed in its annual reports that a small number of customers individually exceeded ten percent of consolidated revenue; in a company whose top line had historically ranged between roughly $20 million and $35 million, the departure or inventory correction of even one such account could reshape a fiscal year's result without warning.

The defence side added a second concentration layer of a different character. US Navy armor programs—centred on HybridTec Armor, CPS's proprietary aluminium-silicon-carbide composite panel system—were awarded episodically through government contracting cycles that bore no relationship to the calendar precision of commercial purchase orders. When a multi-year armor programme was funded and orders flowed, defense revenues inflated the mix meaningfully; when contract vehicles bridged or programme offices delayed follow-on awards pending budget-cycle outcomes, the same revenue line could drop with little advance notice. The result was a business whose two largest demand pools—commercial power electronics and US defense—both exhibited concentration risk, but of structurally different kinds: commercial concentration in customer count, defense concentration in programme timing.

## End-Market Cyclicality

The AI server power-supply thesis that animated much of CPS's commercial narrative through 2024 and 2025 was, at its core, a capex-cycle bet. Hyperscalers—Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta—accelerated data-centre buildout at a pace that drove rack-level power densities past thresholds at which conventional copper heat-spreading became thermally inadequate, opening a larger addressable window for AlSiC baseplates in the power modules that regulate voltage inside AI accelerator racks. CPS benefited from this demand inflection as module makers sourced thermal management substrates for increasingly dense SiC-switched power supplies.

The risk embedded in that narrative was equally straightforward: AI infrastructure capex is demonstrably cyclical. Hyperscaler management teams guided analysts on quarterly calls to the possibility of pause-and-digest phases following periods of concentrated spending; any meaningful deceleration in data-centre investment would translate almost immediately into softer module-maker order books and, with a short lag, reduced AlSiC baseplate pull. Because CPS sold components rather than finished modules, the company sat two tiers from the end customer and was exposed to inventory build-and-burn dynamics at the module level that could amplify swings in end demand.

EV traction inverters introduced an analogous cyclicality risk with a different periodicity. Automotive electrification drove strong demand for SiC power modules through the 2022–2024 period, as tier-one power-electronics suppliers scaled production to serve OEM programmes. But EV demand growth decelerated materially in several major markets, and module makers responded by moderating production schedules, tightening inventory, and deferring component purchases. For CPS, which counted automotive-oriented module manufacturers among its commercial customer base, the EV softness period illustrated how quickly the company's revenue could compress when just one end-market segment revised its near-term outlook.

## Defense Programme Timing

Defense revenues at CPS were structurally lumpy in a way that created earnings volatility disproportionate to the company's absolute size. HybridTec Armor deliveries against US Navy contracts flowed in campaign bursts: when ships were in programme, orders arrived in volume; between programme phases, shipments fell to maintenance levels or paused entirely. Unlike a commercial OEM relationship—where rolling purchase orders create baseline visibility across quarters—a defence armor contract bound CPS to a government delivery schedule that could shift months or years as appropriations, specification changes, or shipyard sequencing intervened upstream.

The mismatch between CPS's fixed manufacturing cost base at Norton, Massachusetts, and the variable, programme-driven cadence of defense revenue meant that armor-heavy fiscal periods produced strong margin and cash generation, while inter-programme troughs required the commercial power-electronics business to carry overhead. In a company of CPS's scale, that swing could be the difference between a profitable and a breakeven year. It also complicated investor communication: management could not always forecast defence revenue with the precision that sell-side analysts expected, a limitation that contributed to earnings surprise volatility and the attendant share-price movement that characterised the stock.

## Small-Cap Scale Constraints

With annual revenues in the $20–35 million range and a single manufacturing campus in Norton, CPS entered the 2024–2026 demand inflection with limited structural capacity to absorb large, rapid demand increases without capital investment. Expanding the near-net-shape forming and infiltration capacity that underpinned AlSiC production required equipment with long lead times and capital outlays that, at CPS's scale, were material relative to its equity base. The company made selective capacity investments through this period, funding them partly through equity raises that diluted existing shareholders without guaranteeing that the associated demand would materialise on schedule.

Scale constraints also manifested in organisational depth. A company generating $30 million in revenue operated with a management team and back-office infrastructure calibrated to that size; winning a large new programme from a major power-module customer or a follow-on Navy armor award required rapid operational scaling that smaller companies executed less smoothly than larger competitors. Supply chain resilience was a related concern: sourcing specialty silicon carbide feedstocks and aluminium alloys in volumes sufficient to serve large order campaigns—while maintaining cost discipline—was inherently harder for a single-plant operator than for a diversified materials group with purchasing leverage across multiple facilities.

## Governance and Capital Structure

CPS Technologies operated as a founder-era small-cap with a governance structure appropriate to its size but carrying the limitations that structure implied. Brian Mackey held the combined President and CEO title through the period under review; the board, as disclosed in successive DEF 14A proxy statements, was compact and included members whose independence classifications and tenure were consistent with the company's NASDAQ listing requirements, though without the committee depth or institutional investor engagement typical of mid-cap peers. Compensation disclosure reflected a straightforward structure, but one with limited long-term incentive complexity, which constrained the tools available to retain and attract technical talent capable of accelerating product development or international customer development.

Capital structure remained modest in terms of debt, reflecting management's historically conservative approach to leverage. Equity raises conducted to fund capacity investment had dilutive effects that were visible in the share count progression disclosed in quarterly filings. In a stock with limited float and concentrated retail and small-institutional ownership, those issuances could pressure the share price even when the underlying capacity investment was commercially sound. The company's access to capital markets was functional but not deep: a large capital need—whether from a capacity emergency or an opportunistic acquisition—would have required execution under adverse conditions.

## Competitive Intensity

CPS's AlSiC franchise faced competitive pressure from two directions simultaneously. Japanese ceramics specialists—principally Kyocera Corporation—offered aluminium nitride and silicon nitride ceramic substrates that competed directly with AlSiC baseplates in high-power-density thermal management applications. Kyocera's scale, manufacturing breadth, and established relationships with Japanese and European power-module makers gave it structural advantages in qualification cycles and pricing discipline that CPS could not match through scale alone. For CPS, differentiation rested on AlSiC's coefficient of thermal expansion matching to silicon carbide chips, its mechanical robustness, and the company's near-net-shape forming capability—advantages that held in specific application windows but were not universal.

A second competitive vector came from global MMC alternatives. European and Asian materials groups pursued their own aluminium matrix composite formulations, and customer engineering teams at major power-module makers continuously evaluated alternative thermal management architectures—including direct-bonded copper on ceramic, vapour-chamber solutions, and advanced polymer composites—as power densities increased and thermal budgets tightened. The proliferation of thermal management approaches meant that CPS's AlSiC solutions, while well-established, competed in a market where the definition of the best-in-class solution was actively contested, and where a specification shift by a tier-one module maker toward an alternative material could strand qualification investments without a clear commercial bridge.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Earnings Clock

CPS Technologies enters the back half of its fiscal year at a structural inflection point. With a fiscal year ending in late June — an unusual cadence inherited from the company's early history — the next twelve months from the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026 span the close of FY2026, a full FY2027 reporting cycle, and the critical period in which management must demonstrate that the AI server and EV SiC demand narratives it has been building translate into durable revenue scale above the historic $20–30 million band.

The immediate catalyst is the fourth-quarter FY2026 earnings release, expected in August 2026. That print closes the books on a fiscal year in which commercial demand — driven by hyperscaler rack-level power density increases and the accelerating adoption of SiC power modules in traction inverters — was the dominant growth narrative. The Q4 result will tell investors whether the demand inflection that began to appear in the company's commercial segment held through the spring quarter and whether design wins that had been in qualification stages converted to volume production pull.

The annual 10-K filing, expected in September 2026, carries secondary but meaningful information density: capacity utilization data, capital expenditure disclosures tied to the Norton, Massachusetts manufacturing campus expansion, and the backlog or order-visibility language that management typically embeds in the filing's business-description sections. For a company of CPS's scale, the 10-K is often richer in operational colour than the quarterly earnings releases.

## Quarter-by-Quarter Catalyst Map

| Quarter | Period | Expected Report | Primary Catalyst |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q4 FY2026 | Apr–Jun 2026 | ~Aug 2026 | FY2026 close; commercial demand durability |
| Q1 FY2027 | Jul–Sep 2026 | ~Nov 2026 | Seasonal reset; new design-win disclosures |
| Q2 FY2027 | Oct–Dec 2026 | ~Feb 2027 | Holiday-quarter power module demand; defense program updates |
| Q3 FY2027 | Jan–Mar 2027 | ~May 2027 | Capacity ramp confirmation; full-year FY2027 pace |

The annual shareholder meeting, typically convened in September or October, is a secondary calendar event: proxy disclosures around compensation structures and any equity-raise mechanics will give investors a view into management's confidence in the revenue trajectory and whether new share issuance is planned to fund further capital investment at Norton.

## Estimates and the Thin-Coverage Problem

CPS Technologies is covered by a small number of sell-side analysts, and the micro-cap nature of the business — market capitalisation historically below $200 million — means the formal consensus is thin and lags primary-source newsflow. Any analyst estimate model built on the historic $20–30 million revenue band required material upward revision as the AI and EV demand inflection became visible in the company's commercial segment through 2024 and 2025.

The implied growth framework, working from structural observations rather than a formal consensus number, suggests FY2027 revenue in the range of $35–45 million represents a credible base-case trajectory if: (a) AI server power module thermal management demand at hyperscaler customers holds at or above the FY2026 exit rate; (b) EV SiC module customer qualifications reached in FY2025–2026 translate into production-volume pulls; and (c) the defense segment, anchored by HybridTec Armor programs with the US Navy, sustains revenue at levels consistent with prior years.

Gross margin trajectory is the key earnings-per-share lever. CPS operates a fixed-cost manufacturing base at Norton — kiln and hot-press capacity is lumpy to add but creates operating leverage as volumes scale through it. Gross margins in the low-to-mid twenties have historically been the baseline; at revenue scale above $35 million, the operating leverage case implies margin expansion toward 25–27 percent is achievable without heroic assumptions. EPS for FY2027 in a base case of $35–40 million revenue and improved margins could approach $0.15–0.25 per diluted share, though with significant sensitivity to the commercial revenue ramp rate and any incremental capital or workforce costs at Norton.

## Management Guidance Framework

CPS Technologies has not historically provided formal full-year revenue or earnings guidance in the manner of larger-cap industrials. Brian Mackey's commentary in earnings calls has tended toward qualitative characterisation of demand environment and order visibility rather than numerical guidance bands. The investor community has come to treat order-backlog language and customer-mix commentary as the de facto guidance proxy.

The absence of formal guidance creates an asymmetric information environment: investors with strong channel checks on the AI power module supply chain and EV module qualification timelines hold a structural advantage over those relying solely on disclosed financials.

## What to Watch Each Quarter

**Commercial revenue growth rate** is the primary thesis-confirmation metric. Each quarterly release should be interrogated for the year-over-year change in commercial segment revenues — defined as power electronics thermal management customers including SiC/GaN power module manufacturers. A commercial revenue growth rate above 20 percent year-over-year would confirm demand inflection continuation. Below 10 percent would raise questions about qualification-to-production conversion timing.

**Gross margin direction** is the secondary metric. Operating leverage on the Norton fixed cost base should become visible as volumes scale. Gross margin expansion of 100–200 basis points per year would be consistent with the thesis; margin compression on higher revenues would signal pricing pressure from customers or input cost headwinds.

**Defense revenue stability** serves as a portfolio ballast metric. The Navy HybridTec Armor and harsh-environment packaging programs tend to follow government fiscal year cycles and program milestone timings. A material drop in defense revenues without a corresponding commercial offset would compress the aggregate revenue trajectory and raise concentration risk questions.

**Capital expenditure cadence at Norton** is a leading indicator of management confidence. Announced or disclosed investments in additional kiln capacity, near-net-shape forming equipment, or cleanroom infrastructure signal that incoming order visibility supports capital commitment. Absence of capex investment signals either saturation of existing capacity at current demand levels or uncertainty about demand durability.

## Beat Versus Miss Framework

A **beat** against current expectations requires two conditions to hold simultaneously: commercial revenue above the implied trajectory (approximately $9–11 million per quarter in the near-term period to support the $35–45 million annual thesis), and gross margin at or above the prior year quarter. A beat on revenue with margin compression is a mixed result that typically drives a muted stock reaction.

A **miss** condition arises from any of three scenarios: a commercial revenue shortfall signalling design-win conversion delays; a gross margin contraction signalling either pricing concessions to key power module customers or input cost inflation not yet offset; or a defense revenue step-down reflecting program completion, sequestration, or budget-timing delays. The most damaging miss scenario combines a commercial shortfall with a margin contraction in the same quarter, as it simultaneously impairs the growth and profitability parts of the thesis.

## The Bull and Bear Setup

The **bull case** is structurally compelling from the frozen snapshot: CPS holds a defensible niche in AlSiC thermal management for which there is no immediately fungible substitute at the dimensional tolerances required by modern SiC power modules. The AI server power supply thermal management demand is secular, driven by rising power density per rack unit that is independent of any single hyperscaler capital cycle. EV SiC module demand is in early innings of a decade-long volume ramp. The manufacturing base at Norton is operating below theoretical capacity, implying revenue can scale with limited incremental capital. A revenue trajectory toward $50 million or above — still well within the theoretical throughput envelope of the Norton campus — at mid-twenties gross margins implies an earnings profile that current valuation multiples do not fully capture.

The **bear case** centres on customer concentration, qualification-to-production timing risk, and the substitution threat. CPS's customer base in power electronics is narrow: losing or deferring a single large SiC module customer to a competing AlSiC supplier or to an alternative thermal management material — silicon nitride-based direct bonded copper substrates being the primary ceramic alternative — could remove a meaningful revenue slug without forewarning. EV market demand timing has proven difficult to forecast; OEM SiC inverter content decisions remain subject to programme delays and platform-level architecture changes. On the defense side, continuing resolution risk in the US federal budget and Navy programme prioritisation decisions could defer or trim armor-related revenues.

The asymmetry at the frozen snapshot date sits modestly toward the bull: the demand drivers are structural and multi-year, the Norton operating-leverage mechanism is well-understood, and the competitive moat in near-net-shape AlSiC processing has not materially eroded. The principal risk is timing — whether the commercial revenue ramp comes through in FY2027 or slips into FY2028 — rather than a structural impairment of the thesis. Investors tolerant of micro-cap illiquidity and quarterly volatility own a different risk profile than the demand story itself implies.

chapters.title: AI power module scaling, EV SiC growth, Navy continuation, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Inflection Moment

By the time the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout reached its most capital-intensive phase in 2024 and 2025, CPS Technologies found itself occupying a position that its founders could scarcely have anticipated when they began pressing aluminum-silicon carbide composites in Norton, Massachusetts four decades earlier. The company's AlSiC baseplates and heat spreaders — unremarkable-looking metal slabs machined to tolerances measured in microns — had become load-bearing components in the thermal architecture of data-centre power supplies running at rack densities that were rewriting the economics of semiconductor packaging. For a company whose annual revenues had historically tracked in a $20-to-$30 million range, the demand signals arriving from power-module manufacturers in 2024 and 2025 represented a structural shift rather than a cyclical uptick.

The mechanism was straightforward even if the scale was not. High-power silicon carbide and gallium nitride power modules dissipate heat at densities that conventional copper or aluminium substrates cannot manage without warping or delaminating over operational lifetimes. AlSiC's thermal expansion coefficient is engineered to match the ceramic substrates bonded to SiC and GaN die, eliminating the fatigue crack propagation that kills module reliability at elevated junction temperatures. As hyperscaler power-supply architectures migrated toward higher-voltage bus designs and 48-volt direct-conversion topologies through 2024 and 2025, the per-unit AlSiC content per server rack climbed with it. CPS's Norton facility, with its proprietary pressure-infiltration forming process, was among the few Western sources capable of supplying net-shape AlSiC components at commercial volumes.

## AI Server Power: From Cyclical to Structural

The inflection in AI server power module demand that gathered force through 2024 and into 2025 was distinguishable from prior cyclical upswings by its customer profile and its duration. Rather than discrete programme wins tied to a single defence contract or a limited consumer electronics design-in, the AI demand signal was spreading across multiple power-module manufacturers who were themselves capacity-constrained by the hyperscaler buildout. Power semiconductor companies serving data-centre power-supply customers — among them the leading SiC and GaN module makers in Europe and Asia — were extending lead times on CPS's components as they sought to secure thermal-management materials ahead of their own production ramps.

The financial structure of the business amplified the operating leverage. CPS Technologies's cost base at Norton is substantially fixed: the infiltration furnaces, the machining centres, and the workforce required to run near-net-shape forming at quality levels acceptable to power-module customers do not scale proportionally with volume. When revenue moves meaningfully above the breakeven threshold, incremental margins on AlSiC components run well above the company-level average. The equity raises that management executed through 2024 and 2025 — adding to the modest capital structure that had characterised the company for most of its history — were directed at capacity expansion intended to capture that operating leverage before competitors could respond.

## Electric Vehicle SiC: A Parallel Ramp

Running alongside the AI server demand signal was a second structural shift in CPS's commercial business: the accelerating adoption of SiC traction inverters in battery electric vehicles. Automotive-grade SiC power modules carry stricter reliability requirements than their industrial counterparts — automotive qualification cycles involve thousands of hours of thermal cycling at temperature swings that industrial applications rarely impose. AlSiC baseplates, precisely because their thermal expansion is matched to the ceramic direct-bonded-copper substrate layers above them, offered the reliability margin that automotive power electronics engineers needed when extending SiC module lifetimes to meet ten-year, hundred-thousand-mile warranty obligations.

The EV SiC ramp presented CPS with a customer profile it had not historically served at scale: automotive tier-1 power electronics suppliers, operating under IATF 16949 quality frameworks, with procurement processes and qualification timelines that differ substantially from the defence and industrial segments the company knew well. Successful navigation of that qualification process was prerequisite to meaningful volume. Through 2024 and 2025, CPS's work to qualify its AlSiC components into automotive SiC module programmes represented a necessary investment in customer diversification — reducing the revenue concentration that had historically made the company's top line sensitive to the timing of a small number of large programme decisions.

## Navy Armor and the Defense Anchor

The defense segment — centred on HybridTec Armor for naval applications and hermetic packaging for harsh-environment electronics — provided a degree of revenue visibility that the commercial side, with its shorter design-in cycles and procurement volatility, could not consistently deliver. US Navy armor programmes, once awarded and funded, tend to run for years under multi-year procurement contracts that insulate revenues from short-term commercial swings. The combination of AlSiC's density and ballistic performance characteristics gave HybridTec Armor a weight advantage over steel-based alternatives that was directly relevant to naval architects managing topside weight budgets on surface combatants.

Defense revenue also served a strategic function within CPS's manufacturing economics: it provided a base-load utilisation of the Norton facility that reduced the risk of the fixed-cost base becoming punitive during commercial programme transitions. When an EV SiC programme slips a quarter or an AI power-supply design-in takes longer to ramp than originally projected, the defense backlog cushions the impact on absorption. That dynamic had operated through multiple commercial cycles over CPS's history, and management's articulation of the two-segment portfolio framework reflected a deliberate choice to preserve the defense anchor even as commercial revenues grew.

GaN RF power packaging — serving both defense electronics and 5G and 6G infrastructure customers — represented a third defense-adjacent revenue thread with its own growth characteristics. GaN RF amplifiers for phased-array radar, electronic warfare, and base-station applications generate heat profiles that demand the same thermal-expansion matching properties as power-module SiC, making CPS's AlSiC substrates a natural fit. Defense electronics spending priorities through 2025, weighted toward electronic warfare and radar modernisation, provided a supportive backdrop.

## Norton Capacity and the Manufacturing Constraint

The binding constraint on CPS's growth scenario through 2026 and beyond was the physical capacity of the Norton, Massachusetts manufacturing campus. Near-net-shape pressure infiltration is not a process that scales instantly: furnaces require qualification, machining centres require tooling and operator training, and the quality systems required to serve automotive-grade customers impose their own overhead on production throughput. The equity capital raised through 2024 and 2025 was directed at expanding that physical capacity, but the lead times involved in bringing incremental capacity online meant that the gap between order intake and deliverable volume could persist for multiple quarters before resolving.

The competitive landscape offered limited near-term relief from alternative Western suppliers. Ceramics-based thermal management alternatives — direct-bonded copper on aluminium nitride or silicon nitride substrates — competed with AlSiC in certain power-module architectures, particularly where the priority was electrical isolation rather than pure thermal conductivity. Companies including Kyocera and other Japanese specialty ceramics manufacturers had established positions in those niches. But AlSiC's combination of machinability, customisability in coefficient-of-thermal-expansion tuning, and cost structure at volume gave CPS a defensible position in applications where the customer needed a metal-matrix baseplate rather than a ceramic substrate.

## The 2026–2030 Horizon

The strategic posture that CPS Technologies carried into the 2026–2030 window rested on three load-bearing assumptions: that AI server power-supply architectures would continue to drive per-rack AlSiC content higher as power densities rose; that automotive SiC traction inverter adoption would sustain demand growth across multiple vehicle platforms and multiple EV powertrain suppliers; and that US Navy armor and defense electronics programs would provide the revenue visibility and manufacturing base-load that allowed the commercial ramp to proceed without fatally exposing the fixed-cost structure.

Against those assumptions sat the risks that any small-cap specialty materials manufacturer faces when growth is concentrated in a small number of customer relationships and programme wins. Revenue in the historic $20-to-$30 million range, even with the operating leverage available at higher volumes, left CPS with limited financial buffer against programme delays or competitive displacement. Customer diversification — across the AI power module, EV SiC, and defense electronics verticals — was the primary risk-management tool available without transforming the company's capital structure or manufacturing model.

The 2024-2025 inflection established the demand case. The years ahead would determine whether Norton's capacity, CPS's customer relationships, and management's execution against a multi-segment growth thesis were sufficient to translate structural demand into sustained financial performance at a scale that rewarded the operating leverage embedded in the business.
